Precise, reversible micro-coils like these point toward soft micro-robots and artificial muscles that work at scales fingers cannot reach.
pmc-13240867:
Aynalem's team looked at how adults in Addis Ababa meet preconception care, years after Ethiopia issued its first national guideline in 2024. Such care still sits outside routine practice. The team spoke with eighteen adults, ten women and eight men, at two public hospitals. Talks explored social, cultural, and structural pressures around preparing for pregnancy.

Seven themes showed knowledge came late, often only after complications struck. Marital gatekeeping, faith beliefs, stigma, and poverty all narrowed access, and single women felt shut out. Men mostly paid the bills but wanted a larger role. People asked for simpler messaging, easier clinic entry, and visible state backing.
pmc-13242367:
Lannon's team in Belfast asked fourteen nurses why weak students pass clinical placements anyway. The nurses assessed students on the wards. Long online interviews probed the 'failing to fail' pattern head-on. All were in postgraduate nursing courses while assessing students. Careful sorting split their accounts into four groups.

Failure carries a stigma that graders dread pinning on a student. Time pressure and thin workplace support squeeze honest skill grading. Close bonds, low grader confidence, and fear of blowback complete the barrier set. Kind workplace cultures, school teamwork, training, and clear guidance enabled firmer calls.
pmc-13242467:
Simone Giovacchini and co-authors tested whether water samples could guide conservation work across freshwater sites in central Italy. Their study appeared in Environmental Management in 2026. Using a DNA test on water from 53 sites, they searched for 11 endangered species, four invasive aliens, one harmful fungus, and one moved fish at the same time. European law already requires member states to track many of these species.

From the results they built three scores that rank sites for protection, for invasive-species removal, and for further survey work. The scores flagged 39 sites as protection candidates, 22 for eradication work, and 33 where DNA surveys would help most. The survey also recorded the target species in 53 map cells where they were not known before. The authors say one combined test can serve several legal duties at once.
pmc-13242967:
Hiroshi Kiyomatsu and co-authors used three-dimensional CT planning to ask which ball size suits reverse shoulder replacements in small shoulder sockets. Their study appeared in Bone and Joint Open in 2026. The patients were Asian women with small glenoid anatomy, a group where implant fit is tight. The team simulated three glenosphere sizes and three amounts of downward overhang in every patient, measuring how far the joint could move before bone met bone.

The smallest ball, thirty-two millimeters, gave the widest arcs in bending, lifting, and rotation, while the largest consistently restricted motion. Placing the ball with at least three millimeters of overhang also helped in every plane. The authors recommend downsizing with adequate overhang for small sockets. They caution that soft tissue and stability, absent from the simulation, must confirm the choice in the operating room.
pmc-13243067:
Chao Meng and co-authors present a 2026 review on how heart muscle heals badly after a heart attack, a process called ventricular remodelling that can lead to heart failure. Their focus is DNA from mitochondria, the cell's energy units, which can leak out and act as an alarm signal.

The authors propose a three-threshold model covering how this DNA escapes, how it travels between cells, and how strongly it switches on an immune alarm pathway. It can move as bare DNA, in tiny cell-made bubbles, or inside whole mitochondria. They suggest timed drug combinations aimed at each step, while noting parts of the model still need direct proof.
pmc-13245067:
Robert Connacher and colleagues asked whether a fruit fly developmental protein must actually grip RNA to do its job. Their study appeared in RNA Biology in 2026. The protein, Brat, guides neural stem cell development and is named for the brain tumors its loss causes. Lab work showed its NHL domain binds specific RNA sites, untested inside a living animal. The team used CRISPR to edit single amino acids at the binding surface, directly in the fly's own gene.

Three independent RNA-binding-defective versions resulted, and each behaved as a strong loss of function. Flies carrying only the edited gene died, mostly as late larvae or pupae, just like flies missing Brat entirely, and the edits failed to rescue known brat mutants. The verdict is clean: RNA binding is not an accessory to Brat's work but its essence. The alleles give biologists a precision tool for separating Brat's roles.
pmc-13246467:
Hasan and co-authors designed an off-grid power system for a coastal island community in Bangladesh, in this 2026 Global Challenges study. Char Ishwar, in Noakhali district, has weak grid access and growing demand. Using planning software, the team modeled a hybrid microgrid combining solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and a hydrogen loop with an electrolyzer, storage tank, and fuel cell to cover calm, cloudy spells.

Of three designs tested for one hundred eighty households, the full hybrid won, delivering power at a modest cost per unit with near-zero net emissions. Wind speed and demand growth most affected the economics. The authors present the design as a practical template for reliable, low-carbon electrification of isolated coastal settlements.
pmc-13247167:
Gong, Fan, Fang, and co-authors built swimming microrobots from living algae in this 2026 Microsystems and Nanoengineering paper. Synthetic microrobots struggle to squeeze through the body's tight, complex spaces, a requirement for reaching tumors. The team instead harnessed Euglena gracilis, a soft, shape-shifting single-celled swimmer, fitting it with magnetic structures so external magnets could steer, propel, and deform it on command.

The biohybrids threaded through dense three-dimensional biological matrices and gathered around tumor spheroids, guided both magnetically and by their own drift toward tumors. The algae themselves add therapy: their chlorophyll supports light-driven tumor killing, and their natural products modulate immunity. The authors present the platform as precision medicine that needs no loaded drug cargo.
pmc-13248967:
Zhang reviewed ultrasound for diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis in this 2026 article. The disease inflames joints and destroys them slowly, and early treatment changes its course. Blood tests miss some patients, especially those whose marker tests come back negative, so imaging that can see inflammation directly has drawn growing interest.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound can reveal swollen joint lining, fluid, increased blood flow, and early bone erosion in real time. It excels at catching hidden inflammation before damage shows elsewhere. Results still depend on the operator's skill, the author notes, but shared scoring systems, standard scanning routines, and early artificial intelligence tools are tightening the method for everyday clinics.
pmc-13249167:
Katayama and colleagues compared two ways blood vessel cells grow old, in a 2026 PLOS One study. Cells can senesce by dividing until they wear out, or early under stress. Both states appear in aging vessels, which grow prone to clots, and the team asked whether the two aging routes affect clotting control differently.

Worn-out cells unexpectedly boosted the vessel lining's anti-clotting behavior in dish tests, while stress-aged cells did not. Mice engineered for stress-aged vessel cells formed worse vein clots, closely matching naturally old mice. Gene patterns agreed. The authors conclude stress-driven aging, not division-driven aging, is the main culprit behind age-related clotting trouble.
pmc-13249567:
Pickersgill and a large drilling expedition team dated the hot water system inside the Chicxulub crater, in a 2026 study. The crater, in present-day Mexico, was blasted out sixty-six million years ago by the asteroid linked to the dinosaur extinction. Heated water circulated through its fractured rock long afterward, the kind of setting where life may first have arisen.

Rock dating and computer simulation together show the hydrothermal activity lasted at least eight million years. That is roughly four times longer than earlier estimates from rock magnetism and mineral studies. The authors call Chicxulub the longest-lived impact-driven hydrothermal system yet documented on Earth, with implications for how life might start on other worlds.
pmc-13249867:
Sato and a Japanese team found a protein that helps the spinal cord rewire after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. Surviving corticospinal fibers, the brain's movement command lines, sprouted into the emptied side of the neck cord and reconnected with V2a interneurons, relay cells for premotor circuits. Silencing those new links chemically weakened the recovered movement, proving they carried real function.

A secreted protein, secretogranin II, rose after injury in helper astrocytes and in the relay neurons during rehabilitation. It pushed axons to grow through familiar growth signals, and removing it blunted rewiring. The authors nominate the protein as a therapeutic lever for stroke and other central nervous system injuries.
pmc-13250167:
Lorenté and co-authors film shock waves moving through a safe stand-in for an explosive. Their 2026 Scientific Reports experiments used compressed sucrose, ordinary sugar pressed into a solid, instead of real energetic material. A short green laser pulse struck the sample to launch each shock wave.

Because the granular material is opaque, the team used high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging to watch the shock form inside it. Follow-up tomography let them estimate the shock pressure and speed, which reached about four times the speed of sound in the material. Adding aluminum nanoparticles made the sample absorb more laser light and raised the pressure. The results point toward detonators triggered by light rather than by impact.
pmc-13250767:
Ruchama Charles and co-authors recount a cancer scare that ended well in this 2026 case report. A 68-year-old man treated two years earlier for colon cancer had rising blood marker levels, and scans found a growing mass inside a hip muscle.

The lump lit up on a PET scan, which raised fears the cancer had spread. Two needle samples gave no answer. Tissue study after closer work showed nodular fasciitis, a harmless, fast-growing knot of repair cells that often mimics cancer. A gene test confirmed it. Since removing such lumps cures them, the authors stress firm diagnosis to spare patients needless cancer treatment.
pmc-13250867:
Lee, Shin, and Song test ear-based nerve stimulation as a drug-free helper for eczema-like skin inflammation in mice. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study uses a chemical called DNCB to trigger atopic dermatitis on mouse skin. Gentle electrical pulses on the ear stimulate the vagus nerve, a pathway known to calm immune responses.

Stimulated mice showed healthier skin structure and lower inflammatory markers than untreated dermatitis mice. Blocking acetylcholine receptors partly erased the benefit, pointing to cholinergic signaling, including one nicotine-type receptor, as part of the mechanism. Treatments ran a few minutes every two or three days for one or two weeks. The authors call the approach a promising add-on and ask for deeper mechanism and translation studies.
pmc-13251167:
Karin Dalhammar, Maria Schelin, and Marie-Louise Möllerberg compare end-of-life care settings in Sweden in this 2026 study. About half of Swedes who die receive municipal care first, and people at home face more emergency hospital trips than those in care facilities.

The study covered 50,219 people in the national palliative care register during 2023 and 2024, all in their last week of life. Facility residents were more likely to get symptom checks than people in ordinary housing. Yet they were less likely to receive end-of-life information, support for relatives after death, or outside pain advice. The authors say each setting has distinct weak spots needing targeted fixes.
pmc-13252767:
Isa Spiero and a large team compare Dutch language models for mining medical notes in this 2026 study. Health records hold rich symptom detail in free text, and automated extraction could save hours of hand labelling, but most tools are built and tested in English.

Two Dutch models were tried on primary care notes from patients with chest infections, against hand-labelled examples. Used as direct classifiers, both did well after enough training, the medical one slightly ahead. Prompt-style use failed badly, with very low scores. Uneven class sizes and missing symptoms dragged performance down, and at least 800 labelled examples were needed. The authors back direct classification for Dutch research use.
pmc-13252967:
Vishal Dalal and colleagues report a heart attack mid-treatment in this 2026 case report. An 80-year-old man arrived with gut bleeding and fainting while taking a blood thinner for a recent leg vein clot, so doctors gave a reversal drug to stop the bleeding.

The reversal drug, since withdrawn from the United States market, was known to raise clot risk days later. This patient, the authors say, is the first known to suffer a major heart attack while the drug was still running into his vein. He had arrived pale and fast-pulsed, with blood counts showing heavy blood loss, and scopes found non-bleeding stomach ulcers that were clipped. The case sharpens warnings around reversal therapy.
pmc-13253767:
Joyce Cristina Freitas leads a 2026 trial on two recovery aids after hard exercise harms muscle. Forty-five active young men were split into four groups: placebo, light therapy, hands-on osteopathic care, or both together. Light therapy used a red LED device, and care was given before a muscle-damage exercise routine.

Blood, strength, flexibility, and jump results were checked up to 72 hours later. Only the combined group had a distinct pattern, with a key muscle enzyme near its start level within 48 hours and a sharp drop by 72 hours. Strength gains were not firm, so the authors treat them as an early trend.
pmc-13253867:
Nehal Ibrahim and colleagues test fruit waste extracts to keep minced beef fresh in a 2026 study. Melon peel, prickly pear peel, and melon seed extracts were made with a green extraction method. The extracts were added to minced beef, and spoilage, germ counts, and taste were tracked over six days.

Melon peel worked best against germs, cutting three bacteria groups by 72, 68, and 51 percent versus plain beef on day six. It also wiped out Listeria by day six. Prickly pear peel gave the best taste scores, while the control beef spoiled. The authors call for cost studies next.
pmc-13258767:
Shalini Purwar and co-authors profile mahua flowers, whose sweetness decides whether they fetch good prices for food and drink processing. Thirteen tree accessions at Banda, India were compared across blooming stages in their 2026 study. Taste, texture, chemistry, minerals, and scent compounds all entered the comparison.

One accession, BM-5, stayed sweetest, richest in minerals, and steadiest in antioxidants as flowers matured. Others stood out only for firmness or springy texture. Gas analysis found over three hundred volatile compounds separating the best and worst accessions. Mature BM-5 brimmed with aroma and fermentation-friendly molecules, marking it as the prime processing candidate.
pmc-13260567:
Ningning Shi and colleagues present a 2026 materials study of nickel-iron phosphide catalysts for water oxidation, the slow half of splitting water to make hydrogen fuel. The study focuses on the promoter role of phosphorus in the catalyst. During operation, the phosphide rebuilds itself into an active nickel-iron oxyhydroxide layer. Phosphorus was found to drive that reconstruction, suppress iron loss, and tune nickel's electronic structure through residual phosphate groups.

Phosphate and iron together act as a redox buffer, preventing nickel from over-oxidizing and stabilizing key reaction intermediates, which lowers the energy barrier. The restructured catalyst needed a low overpotential of 225 millivolts at a standard current density. It also ran stably in alkaline conditions for over one hundred hours at current densities up to five hundred. The authors present phosphorus as a synergistic promoter, not a passive ingredient.
pmc-13262067:
Alejandra Contreras-Manzano leads a team comparing sugary drink intake in Mexico and the United States around new food label rules, in a 2026 journal article. Mexico added front-of-pack warning labels in 2020, while the United States updated its Nutrition Facts labels the same year. The authors tracked whether the two countries then changed in different ways.

They used six yearly surveys from 2018 to 2023, with 24,574 adults in Mexico and 25,019 in the United States. Sugary drink use rose in both countries after 2020, but the rise was smaller in Mexico. Among people who still drank them, amounts, calories, and added sugar changed much the same in both places. Mexican women did show a larger drop in weekly volume.
pmc-13262267:
Mustafa Abdo and colleagues write a 2026 research letter on measuring active lung disease in COPD and in smokers at risk. COPD is a long-term lung disease that limits airflow. They focus on airway wall thickness read from CT scans, and ask what size of change counts as real rather than scan noise or normal variation.

Their plan uses data from the HANSE lung screening study in Germany. They include current and former smokers aged 55 to 79 with at least ten pack-years and two CT scans. A change rule based on spread in the data sorts people into improved, stable, or worse groups. The letter then sets out checking those groups against lung function change and a COPD symptom score, without stating the outcome of that check.
pmc-13262367:
Khalid M Mohany and co-authors test two protective agents against liver harm from a cancer drug in a 2026 journal article. The drug is capecitabine, a pill that turns into a cell-killing agent in the body and can injure the liver. The agents are melatonin, a natural hormone, and cerium oxide nanoparticles, tiny mineral particles.

Fifty male rats were split into five groups, including drug-only and combined-treatment groups, over six weeks. The cancer drug raised liver enzymes, lowered natural defenses, and raised cell-death markers. Each protective agent eased these changes on its own. Together they did best, bringing most measures close to normal and keeping liver tissue close to its normal structure.
pmc-13262567:
Hinako Masumitsu and colleagues unmask a dental material as the hidden trigger behind a woman's repeated allergic crises. Formaldehyde hides in root canal agents, and this thirty-six-year-old patient had asthma and gut allergies muddying the picture. Her 2026 case report tracks eight years of symptoms blamed on the wrong things.

Episodes after dental work grew into swelling, hives, breathlessness, and blackouts, classic anaphylaxis treated with epinephrine. Challenge tests cleared anesthetics, antibiotics, and painkillers one by one. Skin tests and blood antibodies finally pointed to dental products with formaldehyde. Delayed onset, the authors warn, makes this allergy easy to miss for years.
pmc-13262667:
Xavier Ayrignac and colleagues test two blood proteins as trackers for a rare inherited brain disease. CSF1R-related disorder destroys white matter in adults and is often mistaken for other conditions. Stem cell transplants can help, so measuring progression matters. Their 2026 study compares twenty-two patients against several look-alike diseases.

Both neurofilament light chain, a nerve damage marker, and the glial protein GFAP ran high in these patients. GFAP stood even higher than in a genetic frontotemporal dementia group after age adjustment. Within the disease group, both markers rose with disability scores. GFAP also tracked thinking speed and anxiety, strengthening its candidacy for monitoring trials.
pmc-13263367:
Alexander Hayn and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how the structure of tissue around liver cancer cells affects their spread. The tissue scaffold, called the extracellular matrix, stiffens as scarring builds in the liver. The team grew two liver cancer types on collagen and collagen-fibronectin networks of different designs.

They summed up each network with an architectural index combining stiffness, pore size, and fiber spread. As the index rose, cancer cells became softer and more invasive, and they displaced fibers differently. Networks with a high index produced soft, highly invasive cells across both cancer types. The model offers a way to test how structural change in tumors drives aggressive behavior.
pmc-13263767:
SangNam Ahn and colleagues mine nearly two million health records to weigh anxiety and insomnia as dementia risks. Both conditions are common, treatable, and suspected of harming the aging brain. Their 2026 retrospective cohort follows adults over fifty, dementia-free at start, for ten years inside a giant research network.

About two in a hundred participants developed Alzheimer's or a related dementia during follow-up. Insomnia alone nudged risk up slightly, anxiety alone raised it clearly, and having both also elevated it. No subgroup by age, sex, or race behaved differently. Treating sleeplessness and anxiety, the authors suggest, belongs in dementia prevention conversations.
pmc-13264867:
Ho-Young Song led a 2026 study of febrile seizures, fits triggered by fever in young children, and the viruses found alongside them. Virus patterns shifted after the COVID-19 pandemic, and finding several viruses at once is now common. The team asked whether the virus type, or finding many, predicts worse seizures or hospital stays.

They reviewed 558 children aged 6 to 60 months seen at one large children's emergency unit. About 17 percent had complex seizures, the longer or repeated kind. Two virus groups linked to lower odds of complex seizures, and finding more viruses also linked to lower odds, not higher. Nearly half the children carried at least two viruses. The authors urge care in reading multi-virus test results, since more viruses did not mean sicker children.
pmc-13266367:
Mosiur Rahman and a large team wrote a 2026 study of disrespect and abuse during facility-based childbirth in rural Bangladesh. Mistreatment can sour women's view of care and deter future use. The team surveyed 400 women at four community clinics in the Rajshahi area as they prepared to leave after giving birth.

About one in four women, 25.8 percent, reported disrespectful or abusive care across six forms, from physical abuse to abandonment. Risk ran higher for births at night, births without a companion, vaginal and assisted births, women with fewer than four antenatal visits, and the poorest women. Women who reported no such treatment were far more likely to feel satisfied and to recommend the facility. The authors urge action on the named drivers to cut mistreatment in primary care settings.
pmc-13266567:
Racquel McCrary and colleagues present a 2026 case report about a hormone problem found late in pregnancy. The patient was a 36-year-old Spanish-speaking woman, 30 weeks pregnant, with no prenatal care before she arrived. Her parathyroid glands, small glands in the neck, were making too much hormone and raising her blood calcium.

Scans showed excess fluid around the baby, poor growth, and fluid swelling in the baby's body. Fluids and a hormone drug lowered calcium only in part. The baby was delivered early by cesarean section and needed intensive care. After birth, surgery removed the overactive gland and the mother's levels returned to normal.
pmc-13268767:
Maria Ortega Abad and colleagues present a 2026 study of liver care gaps for transgender adults with fatty liver disease. Transgender people face documented care disparities, but liver care was unstudied. At one US medical center, the team identified 254 adults with fatty liver disease by codes and chart review: 85 transgender and 169 cisgender patients, followed across 2015 to 2025.

Transgender patients were much younger, a median of 36 against 57, and more often had the metabolic form of the disease. After adjustments, they had clearly lower odds of gut-specialist consultation, any liver assessment, and advanced liver workup. They also received weight-loss-class diabetes drugs less often, and their body weight rose while controls' did not. The authors call for integrated, inclusive care pathways to close the gap.
pmc-13269167:
Isabella Starling-Alves and co-authors published a review in 2026 on how the brain handles fractions and decimals. These rational numbers trouble many children and adults, yet they matter for school success. The team gathered brain scan studies to find which brain areas switch on during such tasks.

Both fractions and decimals engaged a groove in the side of the brain and front brain areas. Deeper tests suggested the two number forms are still stored in unlike ways. Pooling fraction studies added areas tied to working memory, self-control, and judging size. The authors note that few scan studies target decimals, leaving a clear gap for future work.
pmc-13269467:
Brenna C Duffy, Michael R Nonnemacher, and Sandhya Kortagere published a review in 2026 on how an HIV protein called Tat may drive thinking problems in people with HIV. These problems affect 15 to 50 percent of patients, harming learning, memory, and planning. Tat is made over long periods by infected brain support cells.

The review weighs direct harm to nerve cells against indirect harm through activated support cells. Recent models show Tat switching those cells into states that disturb glutamate, a key signal chemical, by altering its receptors and transporters. Too much glutamate can overexcite and damage nerve cells. The authors argue that studying both routes can point to new treatment targets.
pmc-13269567:
Lucas L Marinho and co-authors wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 on blood markers measured just before hospital discharge in survivors of critical illness. Two simple counts were tested: the ratio of two white cell types, and a low count of lymphocytes, a white cell type that fights infection. The outcome was death within one year.

Records came from a Boston intensive care database covering 2008 to 2022. Of 20,906 eligible survivors, 1,052 had both measures taken within 72 hours before discharge. Their median ratio was 4.2, and 26 percent had the low lymphocyte count. Higher ratios and low counts tracked with greater illness severity and more other diseases. The authors present the markers as cheap tools for spotting higher-risk survivors at discharge.
pmc-13269767:
Giulia Notini and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on Trop2, a surface protein targeted by a class of cancer drugs that carry a poison payload into tumor cells. They combined gene activity data from over 20,000 samples across cancers and healthy tissues. The aim was to learn what controls the target's presence.

The protein's gene was confined to surface-lining tissues, enriched in many tumors, and present in some healthy ones. Gene faults were rare, while a chemical silencing mark tracked strongly and inversely with activity, pointing to that mark as the main control. Activity linked to barrier programs and varied immune contacts. The authors warn that target amount alone cannot predict drug benefit or harm.
pmc-13269967:
Nor Islafatun and Moh Heri Kurniawan published a perspective article in 2026 giving a family caregiver's first-person account of caring for an 85-year-old mother after a left upper limb fracture. The arm was set in a cast, and long recovery at home fell to the family. The piece examines what happened after hospital discharge.

The caregiver describes gaps in follow-up care: local primary services played little clinical role, and referrals ran through paperwork. Families were left to interpret symptoms, watch for decline, and handle new complications without structured guidance. The authors recommend a stronger clinical role for primary care after discharge. They also urge formal recognition of caregivers as partners in planning recovery for older women.
pmc-13270067:
Shailendra Upadhyay and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on treating a fast heart rhythm disorder in patients aged 21 and under without any X-ray guidance. The disorder, AVNRT, is a common rapid rhythm in children, treated by modifying a slow electrical path in the heart. A 3D mapping system replaced X-ray imaging.

The cohort held 125 patients with a median age of 14.9 years, treated from 2016 to 2025. Fluoroscopy time was zero minutes in every case. Acute success was complete, with no procedural complications, and procedures took a median of 121 minutes. Among 117 patients followed for a median of 36 months, the rhythm never returned. The authors support the X-ray-free approach at experienced centers.
pmc-13270667:
Miriam Kesselmeier led a 2026 journal article on POLAR_MI, a German project that hunts for drug risks in patients taking many medicines at once. The work used routine hospital records held at German university hospitals, handled through each site's own data centre to protect privacy.

The team built a two-step method: each centre first gathered and summarised its own data locally, then a central team pooled the summaries. They describe the technical hurdles caused by differing local systems and how repeated rounds of fixes solved them. In the end the pipeline covered ten centres, nearly 800,000 hospital encounters, and about 500,000 patients.
pmc-13270767:
Gamal M. Abdalla led a 2026 prospective randomized trial on cutting early bleeding after sleeve gastrectomy, a weight-loss operation that removes part of the stomach. The trial tested rinsing the staple line with warm salt water before a standard stitching step, against the usual room-temperature rinse.

Between December 2024 and June 2025, 200 adults were split evenly between warm rinse, at body-like warmth, and the cooler rinse. The combined bleeding outcome occurred in 5 percent of the warm group versus 15 percent of controls. Warm rinsing also gave lower drain output and a smaller drop in haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying part of blood, after surgery.
pmc-13270867:

Thirty-five people took part, including 14 youth group members, teachers, health staff, other students, and family members. Members were seen as a bridge between researchers and the community. Taking part seemed to build their confidence, speaking skills, computer skills, and leadership, and the knowledge spread to families and peers. The authors present the group as a model for community-based research partnerships.
pmc-13272267:

Radiomics extracts large numbers of quantitative features from scans, beyond what the eye can see, and might predict outcomes and treatment response.

Searching three databases, the team found thirteen retrospective studies, eleven using machine learning on MRI features. Models from scans before treatment predicted moderately, while models after treatment reached moderate to strong accuracy. One deep learning model of facial nerve outcomes after surgery beat traditional models. Small samples, backward-looking designs, and manual tumour outlining limit the field, the authors note.
pmc-13272567:

They argue the revised German plan favors return advice and buildings, while people with pending claims get mainly short orientation courses. They also fault awarding funds first come, first served, noting that one call was oversubscribed by 30 percent in 27 hours. A minimum open period, a lottery among fit bids, or quality-based awards would be fairer, they say.
pmc-13273067: Correction notice from Samar El Achy and co-authors. It concerns a study of gold particles loaded with a small RNA against liver cancer cells. Figure 7 had an error when first published. The microscope images in panel A were a copy of those in panel C. The original figure and its legend are shown in the notice. The paper has now been corrected.
pmc-13273467:

Monocytes and natural killer cells emerged as key immune subsets, and 23 genes linked causally to the disease. One gene, GNLY, was prioritized, and five candidate compounds bound it well in simulations.
pmc-13274567:

The single-site study plans to follow 170 adults aged fifty to eighty-nine for one year, 115 recently bereaved and 55 matched non-bereaved volunteers. Brain scans at start and twelve months include rest imaging, a face-matching task for emotion, and a stop-signal task for self-control. So far 103 bereaved and forty comparison participants are enrolled and matched, with good-quality scan data collected.
pmc-13274867:
Debiao Luo and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on spotting abnormal network traffic, an early sign of cyberattack. A hybrid neural network then reads the cleaned signal, pairing an attention-based transformer with a memory network that reads sequences both ways.

Tuning such a network by hand is fiddly, so a firefly algorithm, a search method mimicking flashing insects, tuned its settings automatically. On benchmark data sets, the authors report their combined model beat rival and baseline systems on every metric they tested. The gains in prediction error and in the F1 score for catching anomalies were statistically significant.
pmc-13274967:
Tianqing Fan and colleagues present a 2026 prospective cohort study asking whether internet addiction predicts new self-injury in Chinese middle school students. Cross-sectional links were known, but direction over time was not. The team recruited 1,315 students with no history of nonsuicidal self-injury, and 704 completed the six-month follow-up.

Among those followed, 9.8 percent began self-injuring within six months. Risk rose in a straight line with the severity of internet addiction at baseline. After full adjustment, addicted students had about double the odds of starting self-injury. The link was significant in girls, with roughly triple the odds, and in a middle 'internet-dependent' state, but not in boys. The authors urge sex-aware prevention.
pmc-13275767:

Forty-seven healthy adults had one side treated each way, giving ninety-four extractions in total. Three-dimensional face scans measured swelling two and seven days after surgery. The vibration method left less swelling and less jaw stiffness at day two. Pain was lower at every check, and the drill side bled more and needed more painkillers. The new method took longer in surgery, but patients reported less disruption to daily life and higher satisfaction.
pmc-13275967:
Grigorios Avdikos and Stephen Smith wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about heart attacks caused by a fully blocked artery. Some of these attacks never show the classic pattern on an electrocardiogram, the heart tracing called an ECG. The letter comments on a report of three such cases that got delayed artery-opening treatment.

The authors argue the first patient's tracing actually pointed to a different artery than the report claimed. They explain how a common tracing quirk can hide or mimic warning signs in the second case, which they say was very high risk. They close by noting that the usual split between two heart attack types misses many blockages. A newer approach, focused on blocked arteries themselves, could speed up life-saving treatment, they argue.
pmc-13276567:

pmc-13277767: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2025 article comparing the chemistry and biological activity of leaf extracts from spinach and a related plant, Basella rubra. The journal editor-in-chief and the publisher agreed to the retraction over serious concerns about the reliability of the stated authorship and individual contributions. Evidence suggested the article may not have been produced as described. All authors agreed when notified, except one who did not respond.
pmc-13279167:

Risk rose step by step across six blood pressure path groups. Adding the paths to known risk facts sharpened forecasts. The result supports closer watch for those on high paths.
pmc-13279367:

Blood came from fifty cancer cases, half at stage one, plus fifty cirrhosis patients and twenty five healthy peers. A lab method that weighs molecules with high precision measured thirteen body chemicals picked from past work. The write up centres on aims and methods at this stage. Sound early markers could shift care by flagging cancer while treatment can still cure.
pmc-13279567:
Mariana Bezerra Miranda and colleagues give a 2026 systematic review of LED light care for chronic leg wounds. Long lasting leg wounds heal slowly and return often, at high cost. Six trials met the bar, with searches in four databases to May 2026. Light colours spanned red to near infrared, and doses spanned a wide range. Most trials hinted at gains: smaller wound area, better wound bed and more blood flow, most in diabetic foot ulcers. One trial at the highest dose showed no gain. Dose may have a sweet spot, so set dose rules are the next step.
pmc-13280867:
