Chosen simple models predicted dry weight well across species, with noisier results for the diluted optical target. Paired full and pocket-calculator versions suit both automated plants and manual operations.
pmc-13522567:
Giorgia Del Missier, Kiyan Shabestary, and Rodrigo Ledesma-Amaro present a tool paper, published in 2026. It introduces WASP, a pipeline for working out protein functions. WASP uses computed three-dimensional shapes. It does not rely on gene sequences alone. AlphaFold now supplies shapes for most proteins. Comparing shapes can fill label gaps. Matching sequences leaves those gaps even in well-studied species.

In tests, known labels were hidden on purpose. WASP recovered them better than leading sequence-based tools. It labelled a fifth to a third of proteins with no known function. This held across twenty species of practical interest. The authors show its use in curating genome-scale metabolic models for biotechnology.
pmc-13522867:
Ameena M Khan Sullivan and colleagues test how simulated night shifts alter responses to meals in a 2026 laboratory study. Nine healthy young adults who did not normally work shifts completed one day shift and then two night shifts, with sleep and meals delayed by ten hours. Four identical meals were eaten per shift, and blood glucose, insulin, and fats were measured hourly alongside hunger ratings.

Lipid rhythms shifted with the new schedule and flattened noticeably. Night shifts raised glucose and insulin responses after meals, while insulin failed to fully compensate, signaling lower glucose tolerance. Time of day mattered in both schedules, with early evening meals producing the highest glucose responses. The authors propose mistimed eating as one route by which shift work raises metabolic disease risk.
pmc-13523267:
Yujie Shi, Ye Jin, and Hui Yu investigate a small RNA as a marker for newborn breathing disease in a 2026 study. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a major cause of illness and death, especially in preterm infants. Blood and amniotic fluid from thirty-five affected newborns and thirty-five healthy controls were compared for levels of one microRNA, and cell experiments tested its effect on lung surface cells.

The microRNA was elevated in both blood and amniotic fluid of affected newborns, and each fluid distinguished cases from controls with good accuracy. Blocking the microRNA in lung cells improved cell survival and raised output of a key surfactant protein, whose gene it directly regulates. The authors suggest the molecule participates in fetal lung development and could serve as a biomarker for the syndrome.
pmc-13523367:
Patricia González-Berdullas leads a team validating a drug measurement method using saliva and finger-prick blood in a 2026 study. Monitoring the antibiotic linezolid helps balance benefit against toxicity, yet standard monitoring needs venous blood. The new laboratory method measured the drug and its two main breakdown products in oral fluid and in capillary blood collected by a volumetric microsampling device, following international validation guidelines.

The assay performed within accepted accuracy and precision limits across all sample types. In paired specimens from thirty-five treated patients, drug levels in both new sample types tracked plasma levels strongly. Breakdown products behaved less cleanly: they were biased in capillary blood, needing correction factors, and rarely detectable in oral fluid. The authors support the new sampling routes for the parent drug.
pmc-13523467:
Muhammed M. Faiz and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two drugs added to a scalp nerve block for awake brain surgery. Blocking scalp nerves eases pain during awake craniotomy, a procedure where the patient stays conscious, yet a local anesthetic alone wears off quickly. Dexmedetomidine and ketamine were tested as additives to ropivacaine.

Forty-six adults were randomized evenly between the two mixtures. Patients given ketamine waited longer before asking for rescue pain relief, roughly 18.7 hours against 14.7 hours, and reported lower pain scores at several later time points. They also used less rescue medicine. Breathing depression was more common with dexmedetomidine, while that drug better blunted heart rate and blood pressure responses during surgery. The authors call for larger multicenter trials to settle the best choice.
pmc-13525167:
Ong and colleagues tested in 2026 whether swinging reduces academic stress in nursing students. Swinging stimulates the vestibular system, the inner-ear balance sense, and is linked to relaxation. The quasi-experimental study enrolled seventy-eight student nurses in Baguio City, split into swinging and control groups. Stress was measured with a standard academic stress scale, and the team varied swinging duration and body position.

The swinging group showed a significant drop in academic stress compared with controls. How long students swung, and in what position, changed how much stress fell. They recommend building vestibular stimulation into nursing education. That includes campus spaces designed for swinging breaks. The study adds a low-cost, non-drug option to the student stress toolkit, tested across year levels of the nursing programme.
pmc-13525667:
Shiqiong Huang and colleagues run a 2026 retrospective study of adverse drug reactions among hospitalized patients with HIV and AIDS in China, using a variable-selection regression method to hunt for risk factors. Such reactions add heavily to hospital burden in this population. Suspected reactions were judged for causality with an international monitoring system.

Among 918 patients, 210 experienced a reaction, an incidence of 22.88 percent. Blood and lymphatic disorders were the commonest manifestation class. Antibacterial drugs caused the largest share, followed closely by antivirals. The selection model singled out one clear factor, the number of medications given during hospitalization, which raised the odds of a reaction substantially. The authors propose the count as a simple flag for closer monitoring and regimen review.
pmc-13525967:
Salvatore Alessio Angileri leads a large team in a 2026 review of interventional radiology for slipped discs, a common cause of spinal pain and nerve pain. Most patients recover with rest and basic care, yet lasting cases need options between drugs and open surgery. Needle techniques guided by imaging fill that middle step.

A structured search of PubMed and Scopus covered mechanical, thermal, chemical, and healing methods for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar slipped discs. Noted results included pain relief, recovery, complications, and repeat procedures. Findings suggest needle procedures can give real short- and medium-term gains in chosen patients whose symptoms match imaging, with less cutting and faster recovery in skilled hands. The authors note the findings are mostly observational and call for trials across many centers with uniform reporting.
pmc-13528067:
Yongyi Pan and eleven colleagues test a plant compound against obesity-linked male infertility in a 2026 mouse study. Puerarin comes from the kudzu plant root. Mice on a high-fat diet gained weight and made less testosterone. Their sperm counts and movement fell. The team combined gene scans with protein hunting to find the compound's target.

Puerarin trimmed weight gain and fat, and it cleaned up blood lipids. Testes kept a healthier shape, and testosterone, count, and motility rose. The compound latched onto a helper protein called GRP78. That grip steadied StAR, a protein that starts testosterone making. Blocking GRP78 in cells undid the benefit. The authors name the GRP78 to StAR route as the mechanism. Human testing would be a distant next step.
pmc-13528167:
Csilla Kurdi and nine colleagues compare amino acid patterns in egg follicle fluid across three infertility-linked conditions in a 2026 study. The fluid bathes the egg and mirrors body metabolism. Samples totaled 171 from IVF patients. Groups covered insulin resistance, endometriosis, and thyroid trouble. Twenty amino acids were measured with precise lab methods.

Overall patterns looked alike across groups. Disease still left a modest but real fingerprint. Insulin resistance came with lower glycine and arginine. Thyroid trouble came with lower histidine, tryptophan, and lysine. Endometriosis stood out for higher histidine. The shifts held after accounting for body weight. Single amino acids sorted the groups poorly. The authors favor whole-pattern readouts. They say the follicle senses whole-body metabolic health in a quiet, spread-out way.
pmc-13529867:
Shimosato and Goyama review a rare but instructive form of acute myeloid leukaemia driven by rearrangements of the NPM1 gene. The common NPM1 story is a small mutation found in up to two fifths of adult cases, with well-mapped behaviour. Rearrangements, where NPM1 fuses with partners such as MLF1 or RARA, are far rarer and were long neglected. Their 2026 synthesis gathers the emerging evidence on how these fusions look clinically and how they cause disease.

Reassuringly for drug developers, the fusions work through the same machinery as the common mutation. The NPM1 protein ends up stranded in the cytoplasm, partners with the export protein XPO1, and holds developmental HOX genes switched on, driving the leukaemia. Clinically, rearranged cases skew younger and may carry a worse outlook, though the authors flag the small numbers behind that claim.
pmc-13530267:
Mohammad Khorsandi and colleagues test in 2026 green solvents that could dissolve a poorly soluble drug ingredient called 4-hydroxycoumarin. Three acidic deep eutectic solvents, each built from choline chloride plus a simple acid, competed against plain water. Standard shaking-flask measurements spanned a small temperature range.

The propionic acid version lifted solubility more than five hundredfold over water, beating the acetic and lactic versions. Math models fit the data closely, and heating analysis showed dissolving absorbs heat. Cell tests on colon cancer cells found moderate killing power that varied with solvent mix, supporting early drug formulation work.
pmc-13531667:
Silva-Ramos and co-authors combed fleas from rural dogs across 24 municipalities of Cundinamarca, Colombia. They checked them for two bacterial genera that fleas carry to people: Rickettsia, which causes spotted fevers, and Bartonella, behind cat-scratch disease and other illnesses. Colombian data on dog fleas were thin. Their 2026 field study examined 116 dogs in 2019 and 2020, identified the fleas, pooled them, and screened the pools with sensitive DNA tests, following up positives for species identification.

About two fifths of dogs carried fleas, and nearly all the fleas were the cat flea species that happily bites dogs and humans alike. Rickettsia turned up in the large majority of pools, mostly Rickettsia asembonensis with some Rickettsia felis. Bartonella appeared in over a quarter of pools, though sequencing could not pin its species down.
pmc-13531867:
Hongchun Li and colleagues show in 2026 that silencing the Tau protein protects young mice from lasting thinking damage after newborn sepsis. Infection in the first month of life often leaves survivors with cognitive harm into adolescence. Tau, a nerve fiber protein, was the suspect mediator in this mouse work.

Turning Tau down softened memory loss after early inflammation. Brain checks showed reshaped branching in a memory region and renewed birth of nerve cells there in adulthood. The authors nominate Tau as a treatment target for sepsis-related brain injury, with structure and cell renewal as the routes.
pmc-13531967:
Jiangyuan Liu, Johan H Gibcus, and Job Dekker present in 2026 a workflow that calls DNA loops jointly across related chromosome-folding datasets. Loop calls from Hi-C maps vary wildly between similar samples, muddying comparisons. Their tool, UnionLoops, first builds one shared candidate set, then applies uniform filtering and scores support sample by sample.

Joint calling found more shared loops, trimmed spurious one-off calls, and matched independent protein occupancy evidence better than single-sample routes. Cleaner loop maps sharpen reading of how genome folding shifts across conditions, a basic need for studies of development and disease across sample groups.
pmc-13532867:
Yanqiu Wang and colleagues tested what happens while focused ultrasound is beamed at the brain's movement area, rather than after it ends. They measured how strongly one side of the brain reins in the other, a balance key to smooth movement.

Fifteen healthy volunteers received ultrasound to one movement area while magnetic pulses measured the cross-brain braking at two time gaps. Ultrasound weakened the long-gap braking from the treated side to the opposite side during the beaming. The short-gap braking stayed unchanged, and the opposite side's own excitability did not shift either. Wang reads this as ultrasound tuning a complex circuit, and offers it as a probe of how the two brain halves interact.
pmc-13534667:
Mengyue Wei and colleagues optimise in 2026 an ethanol extract of Litsea cubeba fruit and probe how it kills Staphylococcus aureus. The plant has a long history as a spice and folk remedy, and natural germ killers are sought for food and drug use. Response surface methods tuned heat, time, and liquid ratio for the best yield.

Best settings gave a high antibacterial rate, and chemical scans found 20 compounds led by fatty acids. The extract killed germs at low doses and broke their walls and membranes, leaking cell contents. The work supports the fruit as a natural antibacterial source.
pmc-13534767:
Mónika Koós and a large global team develop in 2026 the Paraphilic Disorders Short Screen, a brief tool aligned with current ICD-11 rules. No reliable screen existed for these disorders under the new guidance. Data came from 82,243 adults across 42 countries in 26 languages, with expert-led item design.

The screen covers seven paraphilias in 21 items, with cut scores set per guidance. Voyeuristic interest was most common, and groups meeting disorder cut-offs showed worse depression and anxiety than others. Clinicians and researchers gain a validated way to flag at-risk people across cultures.
pmc-13536267:
Michael Rouse, Yumna Kaleem, and Justin M Yeung discuss in 2026 how artificial intelligence can lower barriers to research for surgical trainees. Research is now core to training, yet cost, time, thin mentoring, and ethics delays block many juniors. Their view maps AI help across each research stage.

Tools can aid idea shaping, literature search, protocol drafting, ethics forms in plain language, data extraction, and analysis code. The authors stress that AI should support, not replace, core skills like design judgement and critical reading. Risks and limits must stay in view for safe trainee use.
pmc-13536767:
Laura Barberán-Bernardos, Miguel Ángel Ariza-Gracia, and David P Piñero compare two eye imaging devices in a 2026 agreement study. Both devices measure front eye shape, corneal thickness, and chamber size used in diagnosis and surgical planning. Fifty-five healthy eyes were measured with each device by the same examiner. Paired tests and agreement plots assessed whether readings could be swapped in practice.

Front corneal curvature agreed well enough for shared use, with no clear average gap. Other measures differed clearly, including back curvature, chamber depth, thickness, and chamber angle, with one device tending toward deeper chambers and narrower angles. Thickness agreement ranges were wide. The authors warn against swapping devices freely for thickness checks before lens surgery or for chamber measures guiding implant choices.
pmc-13536867:
Zichun Wang and colleagues track care delays for migrant tuberculosis patients in suburban Shanghai in a 2026 review of cases from 2015 to 2024. Two delays matter, the wait before a patient first seeks care and the wait before the system confirms diagnosis. Records held 3,178 lung tuberculosis cases, split almost evenly between locals and migrants in Fengxian District. Trends and risk factors for each delay were compared.

Migrants waited fewer days before seeking care than locals, yet waited longer for confirmed diagnosis. The first wait among migrants rose steadily from 2017 onward. Female sex, middle age, and first seeking care outside the district raised the first wait, while test results and care location shaped the second wait. The authors urge better cross-district coordination and stronger local lab testing.
pmc-13538567:
Abdalla Elbialy presents a framework that sharpens spot-based tissue gene maps to single-cell detail without outside references in a 2026 study. Spot platforms average several cells per reading, while rival sharpening tools need reference data or fresh training per dataset. The morphology-guided system works training-free, validated on one colon cancer sample measured across four platforms, including a true single-cell reference.

On the finest spot input, the system matched the single-cell reference more closely than any rival tested. Across six distribution checks on a shared gene panel, its variants led most metrics with no rival winning any. Trained rivals merely tracked raw readings on matched regions. The authors highlight per-cell records with coordinates as output no raw spot reading can supply.
pmc-13540867:
Weishan Lin leads a 2026 study explaining part of the bone fragility seen in spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that wastes muscle and leaves many patients with osteoporosis. Muscle talks to bone partly through tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, and patient muscle samples hinted that this traffic was disturbed.

Patients and model mice both showed muscle releasing far fewer vesicles. Those vesicles, when supplied in adequate doses, encouraged bone-forming cells and restrained bone-eating cells just as well as vesicles from healthy muscle, and replenishing them rescued bone in the mice. The chain ran from the missing SMN protein down to a release protein, SNAP23, whose fall throttled vesicle secretion.
pmc-13540967:
Laura L Jelliffe-Pawlowski leads a 2026 California study building an index of preterm birth risk that only counts risk factors medicine can actually act on. Preterm birth is the leading killer of young children, and proven interventions for many maternal conditions reach fewer than half of eligible women.

Linked records for 1.9 million singleton births between 2016 and 2020 were split into training and testing sets. Eighteen candidate risks with evidence-based responses, spanning clinical, behavioural, and social domains, fed the index. Conditions such as chronic hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, asthma, and mental illness anchor the list. The study examines how well the index flags risk through pregnancy and which factors combine most dangerously.
pmc-13542067:
Hilal Kalkan and seven colleagues monitor, in a 2026 field study, whether pole vaulters keep their run-up speed across repeated attempts as effort builds inside the body. Approach speed in the final metres is the main mechanical driver of jump height, so any fade matters to coaches.

Eleven competitive vaulters, four women and seven men, made four jumps twenty centimetres below their personal bests with short rests. Blood lactate and heart rate stayed statistically flat between attempts, while felt exertion rose only late in the set. Run-up speed and every step measure held steady throughout. The authors conclude that this submaximal protocol preserves speed even as internal signals climb unevenly.
pmc-13543467:
Xueqin Shi and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective study building a metabolic risk profile for children and adolescents with obesity, combining hormone measures with common gene variants. Records from 2021 to 2025 supplied 429 young patients, whose clinical, blood, and endocrine data were reviewed alongside genotyping at three obesity-linked sites in the FTO, MC4R, and LEPR genes. Metabolic syndrome was judged by paediatric criteria, and models tested which factors predicted it.

Nearly forty-four percent met the syndrome definition. Insulin resistance was widespread even before puberty and was strongly tied to the syndrome. Higher leptin, a fat-derived hormone, raised risk, while higher adiponectin lowered it. Carrying risk versions of FTO or MC4R each independently predicted the syndrome as well. A combined hormone-and-gene model separated cases reasonably well, suggesting clinics could flag high-risk children with obesity earlier than symptoms alone allow.
pmc-13544967:
Murad-Kassam and colleagues review hospital experiences of older adults with dementia from ethno-racial communities in this 2026 scoping review. Dementia care in hospital is often complicated by racism, stigma, staff bias, and a lack of culturally and linguistically suitable services. Searching six databases, the team gathered studies about patients aged 60 and over and their caregivers, with no limits on year or country.

Only eleven studies qualified from an initial 3,395 records, itself a sign of how thin the evidence is. The findings grouped into five areas. They covered factors before admission and care during the stay. Discharge and readmission formed another area. So did gaps in culturally tailored practices and challenges faced by caregivers. The authors describe a persistent failure to provide culturally focused dementia care across the whole hospital journey and call for research following families through it.
pmc-13545067:
Manfredi and co-authors review how speech and language break down across childhood psychiatric disorders, in this 2026 article. They also review what brain imaging reveals about why. Language supports social ties. So its breakdown in autism, schizophrenia, ADHD, and depression carries consequences far beyond vocabulary. Yet the neurobiology in young people remains patchily mapped.

The authors survey systematic reviews and first studies. The studies used EEG, MRI, and near-infrared spectroscopy. Every condition looked at shows both altered speech function and matching brain changes. The evidence base is lopsided, though. Autism leads the child literature. Schizophrenia and depression research mostly recruited adults. Those fields simply assumed developmental continuity. The central message is a gap statement. The neural causes of the alteration in developing psychiatric populations are largely not studied. They deserve dedicated child and adolescent imaging work.
pmc-13545567:
Tingting Jiang and colleagues described in 2026 a difficult case of chyle fluid collecting around the lung after a double lung transplant. The patient, a 31-year-old woman with a rare lung disease, developed the collection 39 days after surgery. An earlier attempt to seal the space instead left a honeycomb of separate pockets that ordinary drains could not reach.

Dissolving the pocket walls with a clot-breaking drug is risky so soon after transplant, since bleeding could damage delicate surgical joins. The team used contrast-enhanced ultrasound to tell bloodless fibers from living tissue, then injected a low dose of urokinase only where it was safe. Drainage and repeat sealing followed, the lung re-expanded fully, and the problem did not return.
pmc-13546267:
Yang Zhi and co-authors reviewed in 2026 what is known about the Notch1 signaling pathway in diabetic foot. In this serious complication, nerve damage, poor circulation, and slow healing can lead to amputation. Notch1 passes messages between neighboring cells and helps govern blood vessel growth, inflammation, and cell fate. Evidence gathered in the review links faulty Notch1 activity to several of the processes that keep diabetic foot wounds open.

The authors walk through the pathway's roles in vessel formation, immune response, nerve injury, and tissue repair, then survey treatments that try to adjust its activity. Their aim is to give researchers a clearer map of the mechanism and to point toward targeted therapies for ulcers that resist standard care.
pmc-13547367:
Hui Li and colleagues traced in 2026 a chain of molecular switches that slows prostate cancer when one long non-coding RNA is present. Both that RNA, LINC00222, and a protective gene it controls, FOXO3, run low in prostate tumors. Raising FOXO3 in cancer cells shifted them toward a less mobile state and made them more sensitive to the chemotherapy drug docetaxel.

The RNA works by soaking up a small regulatory molecule that would otherwise silence FOXO3. Freed FOXO3 then raises a partner protein that reins in the beta-catenin growth pathway. Raising LINC00222 in cells slowed growth and spread while raising cell death, and animal experiments confirmed the braking effect. The authors present the chain as a candidate route for new treatments.
pmc-13548067:
Marco Tozzi and colleagues showed that brown fat cells release the energy molecule ATP when adrenaline-like signals switch them into heat-making mode. The released ATP then amplifies the very signals that freed it. Brown fat burns fuel to produce heat in the cold. Working with cultured brown fat cells and mouse tissue, the team tracked ATP release in real time and measured oxygen use, sugar breakdown, and fat splitting.

Release ran through a channel protein called pannexin-1 under control of the cell's main adrenaline relay. Glucose raised release while insulin trimmed it. Blocking the channel or mopping up outside ATP weakened the fat-burning responses, and both ATP and adrenaline raised calcium signals on different schedules. Cold exposure reshaped the tissue's ATP receptor mix.
pmc-13548467:
Alexandre Bourdiol and a French study group laid out in 2026 the DEXA-BURN trial protocol, testing whether an early course of the steroid dexamethasone can cut major complications after severe burns. Badly burned patients suffer intense, lasting inflammation with frequent lung and kidney failure, yet no large trial has tested steroids in this group. The double-blind trial runs in ten French intensive care units.

Adults with burns over at least a fifth of the body who arrive within a day and need a ventilator will be randomized to five days of intravenous dexamethasone or a placebo. The main measure combines serious lung injury and kidney injury within 28 days, with deaths at 90 days tested next in a fixed sequence. Enrollment targets 478 patients, and side effects of steroids are tracked closely.
pmc-13548567:
Wenfan Gao and colleagues examine what drives blood levels of olanzapine, a widely used schizophrenia medicine, in a 2026 retrospective study of 104 Chinese patients. The drug's levels vary greatly between people, and it often disturbs metabolism. After four weeks of treatment, the team compared drug concentrations and dose-adjusted levels across sex, age, and body mass groups, then checked links with metabolic measures and inflammatory proteins.

Women carried higher drug levels and higher dose-adjusted levels than men. Heavier body mass went with lower raw levels, while age showed no clear effect. Metabolic measures did not track with drug levels during this short window. Higher drug levels instead went with lower levels of three inflammatory signals, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. The authors suggest sex and body size deserve attention when dosing, and that inflammation links merit longer study.
pmc-13550467:
Li and colleagues re-sequenced in 2026 the genomes of 984 soybean lines to map structural variations, large DNA changes such as insertions and deletions, and link them to crop traits. Such variants shape many traits but were poorly charted in soybean. Combining their 940 new sequences with public data, the team built a graph-based genome, a reference that holds many variant paths at once, to catch changes a single reference misses.

Li catalogued over 600,000 structural variants plus tens of thousands of presence-absence changes that affect gene activity widely. The variants proved a core force in soybean domestication and later breeding gains. Trait mapping pinned down concrete cases: inserted jumping genes that alter seed coat colour, insertions in a pigment gene that change flower colour, and a deletion that enlarges seeds. The map gives breeders a resource for faster, targeted crop improvement.
pmc-13551767:
Betül Esra Çevik and Hümeyra Hançer Tok published a 2026 randomized trial of fall-prevention education for older adults in Türkiye. Sixty-six adults attending a family health center in Central Anatolia, all classed high risk on a standard fall scale, joined the pretest-posttest study. The intervention group received two interactive sessions with presentations and discussion, while controls received only an information brochure.

Safe fall behavior scores rose significantly in the taught group and did not move in the brochure group in the reported comparisons. Post-test scores also separated the groups in favor of teaching. The authors conclude that passive leaflets do not change behavior, while nurse-led interactive education does, a practical point for clinics serving high-risk older adults.
pmc-13551967:
Ana R. Silverstein and thirteen colleagues reported in 2026 on a mitochondrial DNA variant tied to immune differences between the sexes. Scanning mitochondrial variants against traits in a large United States aging study flagged one variant linked to sex-specific immune composition. Because the mitochondrial genome was recently re-annotated to include tiny protein-coding segments, the team could map that variant to a small gene encoding a previously unknown microprotein.

They named the microprotein MASL and confirmed the variant's immune links in two large cohorts using phenome-wide scans. A targeted sequencing method showed sex differences in gene expression near the variant, and blood levels of MASL itself differed by sex in the reported measurements. Synthesized MASL also acted differently in male and female mice, opening a new corner of mitochondrial biology.
pmc-13553667:
Amanda Liesegang, Andy Wu, Alexander Heriot, and Glen Guerra review the rarer inherited conditions that fill the colon with polyps. Their 2026 review leaves aside the two best-known syndromes, Lynch syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis. The rarer forms overlap in looks, vary in how often cancer follows, and rest on a thin proof base. The authors searched two large databases and wove the findings into plain guidance.

Gene testing with wide panels has reshaped the field, naming new syndromes passed down in dominant and recessive ways. Advice on how often to scope the bowel still differs between sources. Open questions cover true cancer risk, best timing for action, and drugs that might prevent polyps. The authors call for shared registries, forward-looking data, and agreed guidelines.
pmc-13554067:
Katarzyna Gościnna leads a seven-author team studying how farm choices shape the health value of potatoes in a 2026 report. Trials ran during 2020 and 2021 on two table varieties, Gardena and Denar. The team varied nitrogen feed, spray protection, a growth booster, water-storing gel, and extra watering. They then measured polyphenols, plant compounds tied to health, plus strength against cell damage.

Variety mattered most, with Gardena holding roughly a quarter more polyphenols on average. A mid-high nitrogen dose gave the richest tubers for both varieties. Full spray protection with a silver-based seed dressing also scored well. Extra watering paired with the booster lifted both polyphenols and protective strength. The authors praise Gardena as a strong Polish variety for European farms.
pmc-13557867:
Xu Jiang and twelve colleagues trained in 2026 a deep foundation model to spot hidden lymph node spread in early small cell lung cancer from ordinary CT scans. About a third of patients who look node free before surgery prove to have occult spread afterwards, and that finding worsens survival and changes treatment. The multicentre study drew 416 surgically treated patients whose scans preceded operations at five hospitals.

Images from the largest centre trained and internally tested the model, while the other four centres formed an outside test set. Deep features pulled from a cancer-pretrained foundation model fed standard classifiers, and performance was compared with handcrafted image features, ordinary neural networks, and a clinical model. The foundation approach was built to be interpretable as well as accurate. The authors present it as decision support for staging and surgical planning.
pmc-13558567:
Ramkumar Sivasakthivel and six colleagues presented in 2026 a neural network that reads forearm muscle signals to recognise hand gestures. Such systems power prosthetic hands and touch-free controls, yet muscle signals vary in timing and across electrodes in ways that trip simpler models. Their design stacks residual learning at several time scales with a squeeze-and-excitation module that reweights which signal channels matter for each gesture.

Signals from a public gesture dataset were cleaned with standard filtering, scaling, and sliding windows, then split into training and test portions. The network learned both fast and slow temporal patterns while emphasising informative channels, which the authors credit for its classification gains over earlier machine learning and deep learning approaches. They frame the architecture as a step toward more reliable wearable gesture interfaces for assistive devices.
pmc-13559467:
María Teresa Zarco-Martín and three colleagues examine whether muscle mass and strength predict survival in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease defined by progressive muscle wasting. Their prospective cohort study ran at a multidisciplinary ALS unit in Granada, Spain, and enrolled 42 patients. Muscle status was gauged by impedance analysis, ultrasound, grip strength, and a short physical performance battery.

During follow-up, 45 percent of the patients died. Those who survived carried more appendicular muscle for their height and gripped more strongly, while body mass index alone showed no difference. Sarcopenia, the combined loss of muscle and function, appeared far more often in those who died. One muscle index discriminated survival best, with an area under the curve of 0.81 in the reported analysis. The authors argue that checking muscle status adds warning information beyond weight, and that sarcopenia flags a subgroup at especially high risk.
pmc-13559567:
Tingting Qi, Jing Yang, and Guzhalinuer Abulizi investigate CEBPG, a transcription factor suspected of acting as an oncogene in cervical cancer. Their 2026 study first reads the factor's levels in cancer atlas data, then forces extra CEBPG into HeLa cervical cancer cells and watches the consequences. Gene sequencing after the change maps which genes the factor controls.

CEBPG ran markedly higher in cervical tumors than in normal tissue. Cells given extra amounts multiplied faster, migrated and invaded more readily, and resisted programmed cell death. Sequencing revealed many shifted genes concentrated in pathways for blood vessel growth, proliferation, and movement. The analysis nominated 27 likely direct target genes, several already tied to poor prognosis in this cancer. The authors frame CEBPG as a driver of malignant behavior and a candidate biomarker. Their functional evidence, though, comes from a single cell line.
pmc-13562667:
Huixuan Li and seven colleagues pair reinforcement learning with robust optimisation to run clusters of linked microgrids under uncertainty. Solar output, demand, and prices all swing, and plans built on one forecast can fail expensively. The 2026 framework works on two levels: learning agents for each microgrid chase long-run rewards, while a lower layer dispatches power and trades energy between grids under operating limits. A robust layer, built around the Wasserstein distance, guards against real data drifting from the assumed pattern.

Trials used a five-microgrid system with solar panels, batteries, and loads across 300 past scenarios. Running cost fell by 14.8 percent against deterministic, stochastic, and learning-only rivals. Resilience climbed from about 85 to 96 percent, and the chance of failing to meet load dropped from about 5 to 2 percent. Performance held near optimal as the safety margin widened. The authors promote the hybrid as a route to self-running grids.
pmc-13563667:
Fengke Sun and seven colleagues film the life of a hole inside a photocatalyst crystal, from birth to the moment it does chemistry. Photocatalysts promise fuel from sunlight, yet most light-made charges die before reaching the surface. The 2026 team used a transient reflection microscope, watching crystals of bismuth vanadate while reactions ran. Their crystal faces were shaped in advance to steer charges apart. Timings resolved down to trillionths of a second let them separate steps that older tools blur.

Holes split from their electron partners within about 5 picoseconds. They then fell into trap states after roughly 1.5 nanoseconds, and those traps, sitting at oxygen sites on the surface, handed the holes to water molecules in about 19 picoseconds. Direct injection from the main band barely happened. The authors recast trap states as the relay stations that make surface chemistry fast, a design hint for solar fuel materials.
pmc-13563767:
Yuki Someya and four colleagues follow former college athletes into middle age to ask whether the enlarged athlete's heart of youth ever turns into disease. That training enlargement is supposed to melt away after retirement. Their 2026 study analysed 980 alumni of Juntendo University, average age 52, who reported their college heart history in a 2018 questionnaire. They also gave DNA for a gene variant in the ACE gene, a blood-pressure regulator. 177 alumni, 18.1 percent, recalled an athlete's heart, and 15 later developed left ventricular hypertrophy.

Those with an athlete's heart history carried 7.3 times the prevalence of later hypertrophy. The gene sharpened the story: carriers of the D version of the variant who also had the youthful enlargement showed odds of 13.63, though the estimate rests on few cases. The authors suggest that former athletes with both markers merit heart checks in later life, rather than assuming the enlargement was harmless.
pmc-13563867:
Sheng Li and four colleagues survey nearly ten thousand nurses about workplace violence and how their coping habits bend its damage. Nurses meet aggression from patients and families more than almost any workforce, and wellbeing suffers. Their 2026 study questioned 9,466 nursing staff from over fifty hospitals in Lanzhou during February and March 2025. Hierarchical models tested whether a positive, problem-facing coping style shields wellbeing, and whether a negative, avoidant style deepens the harm.

Violence exposure predicted lower occupational wellbeing, though the raw link was weak, hinting at hidden suppression in the data. Positive coping strongly raised wellbeing and negative coping dragged it down. Under heavy violence, positive coping's protection faded while negative coping's harm grew stronger, a double squeeze on the most exposed staff. The authors urge tiered support: organisations should aim coping training and backup first at high-exposure units, rather than offering the same programme to everyone.
pmc-13566467:
Nanouk Zuidmeer, Jori Symons, and Monique Nijhuis review, in a 2026 article, how HIV persists in microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, even when treatment suppresses the virus in blood. Microglia can carry complete, wakeable copies of the virus, tucked into different chromosome spots than in blood immune cells.

Infected and even nearby uninfected microglia turn inflammatory and age-like, feeding brain injury, and therapy calms but does not fully reverse that state. Cure efforts, the authors argue, must reach this brain reservoir and quiet viral activity there. The review sets priorities for researchers aiming at a complete HIV cure rather than control alone.
pmc-13571367:
Akash Dontamsetty and colleagues report, in a 2026 case, an 81-year-old woman whose prolonged seizures triggered takotsubo syndrome in both ventricles. Takotsubo is a stress-related heart failure that imitates a heart attack. She arrived after a major convulsion, then developed hidden ongoing seizures, shock, and severe heart weakness with pumping strength under twenty percent.

Her pumping strength later recovered to the normal range, confirming the reversible pattern. Her course still grew worse with a small lung clot, breathing failure, confusion from metabolic problems, and muscle weakness from critical illness needing rehab. The authors urge early heart checks whenever prolonged seizures destabilize a patient.
pmc-13572167:
Guo and co-authors fed a 2026 comparison of dietary oils in Pekin ducks, testing soybean oil against flaxseed oil and rubber seed oil for omega-3 enrichment. One hundred and forty-four day old ducks were split into three groups and fed the diets for six weeks. Fatty acid make-up, antioxidant status, and liver gene activity were measured at the end.

Both alternative oils cut liver and abdominal fat indices and enriched omega-3 fats in blood and liver while lowering the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio. Rubber seed oil outperformed flaxseed oil on most measures Guo reports, dropping blood triglycerides, cholesterol, and a liver enzyme significantly. It also lowered a fat damage marker in blood and liver while boosting several antioxidant enzyme activities. Liver genes for fat burning fell and protective genes rose under both alternative oils.
pmc-13572367:
Hemant Kumar Sharma presents a 2026 theory study of charge flow through a tiny device made of three quantum dots set in a triangle. Such a device works like a very small transistor built from a single molecule. The study asks how three forces shape the flow: electrons pushing on each other, electrons linked to shaking in the dots, and loss of that shaking to the base below.

Sharma uses a math model that treats the link to shaking in full, not as a small tweak. A Green's function method then yields the charge spectrum, the current, and how current changes with voltage. The results show how charge push-back, reshaped energy levels, and damping act together. The work maps when flow stays smooth, when shaking helps it, and when loss to the base dulls it.
pmc-13572567:
Anjali Rathee, with ten colleagues, reports a 2026 study of loneliness and care satisfaction in stem cell transplant patients. Transplant patients spend weeks in protective isolation to dodge infection, and that confinement can weigh on mood and trust in care. The team asked who feels isolation most, and what softens it.

The study enrolled 47 adults at a large hospital in India after autologous or allogeneic transplants. Set scales gauged felt isolation and satisfaction with care. Near half the patients fell into a high-isolation group, and a like share scored low on satisfaction. A caregiver who was not the patient's partner was the strongest marker of high isolation. Being unmarried marked the lowest satisfaction. The caregiver effect on satisfaction ran fully through how patients felt about their ties with others.
pmc-13575267:
Sounira Mehri and Josef Finsterer wrote this 2026 letter responding to a study by Oh and colleagues. That study used exome sequencing and mitochondrial DNA analysis in 77 children with blood or protein in the urine and a family history of kidney disease. It reported a yield of 55 percent, with COL4A-related kidney disease the commonest finding. Mehri and Finsterer welcome it but challenge how gene variants were judged harmful.

They argue that prediction tools alone cannot prove a variant causes disease: tools disagree, and their accuracy is low for several variant types. Proof needs patient features, population frequencies, family segregation or lab function tests. They fault the handling of a symptom-free carrier of a mitochondrial variant known for multi-system disease. Such carriers need brain, eye, ear and heart screening, they write. Low mutation levels in blood do not rule out illness, so follow-up is essential.
pmc-13578167:
Elizabeth Dudnik leads a 2026 phase II trial of first-line chemo-immunotherapy for advanced large-cell neuroendocrine lung carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer with little trial data. Patients received durvalumab, an immune therapy, plus platinum and etoposide chemotherapy for four cycles, then durvalumab alone on a monthly schedule. The main goal was the share of patients free of progression at twelve months.

The trial closed early for slow recruitment after twelve of twenty-two planned patients joined. Median time without progression was 4.4 months, while the twelve-month progression-free share reached 25.0 percent, above the bar the design set. Half the patients' tumours shrank measurably, and all three patients with untreated brain spread saw it clear completely inside the skull. Side effects were mostly mild, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results consistent with their hopes, while stressing the small numbers.
pmc-13578267:
Wonyong Kwun and co-authors describe a 2026 rapid test for scabies, the itchy skin disease caused by a tiny mite. Standard checks rely on scraping skin and hunting for mites under a lens, a method that misses many cases. Their test copies mite DNA at one steady heat, so it needs little gear and no full lab.

A quick lysis step frees DNA straight from scrapings, skipping the usual extraction work. Two mite gene targets each lit up within about half an hour, and neither fired on human DNA or on dust mite DNA. Scrapings from patients with classic and crusted forms tested positive, while control skin stayed negative through many repeat runs. The team pitches the kit for clinics and field care.
pmc-13579767:
Luyao Ma, Tongxi Hu, and Jinjuan Huang report gut bacteria carrying a plasmid with a potent drug breaking gene, found in a patient with a torn intestine, in a 2026 study. Three strains of an environmental species, Comamonas thiooxydans, grew from diarrheal samples on plates laced with a last line antibiotic. Gene checks confirmed each strain carried a metal based enzyme that disarms that drug class.

Full genome reads placed the gene on a movable plasmid, not the main chromosome. One early strain also held an extra DNA insert with a regulator gene. Set against 481 related genomes, the isolates proved distinct from one another yet closest to a strain from the environment. The authors warn this species may warehouse and shuttle resistance genes inside the human gut, and they urge watch lists to include it.
pmc-13581467:
Louiza Papantonatou and colleagues compare two gum thickening methods placed with dental implants in the smile zone, in a 2026 trial. Twenty five patients were assigned by chance to a collagen matrix, a graft of their own connective tissue, or no thickening. Ultrasound tracked gum thickness and cone beam scans tracked the bone plate, at placement and six months on, with tissue samples and patient reports added.

Both graft types thickened the gum clearly over doing nothing, with the matrix slightly ahead on paper. The bone plate thinned over time in every group, so thickening the gum did not save bone. Patients rated both routes much alike, though the own tissue graft stung a bit more. Lab views showed both materials settling in well. The authors call for bigger trials to settle the pairing.
pmc-13582767:
Shir Ginosar Yaari, Noa Boker Segal, and Maya Tamir test whether feeling worse makes a person worse at cheering someone else, in a 2026 study. Two experiments paired a helper with a person facing an upsetting stimulus. In one, sixty four pairs of strangers took part; in the other, one hundred ten pairs of closer partners. Helpers rated their own feelings, then tried to lift the other person's mood.

The pattern held in both rounds. Helpers who reacted more strongly left their partners feeling worse than calmer helpers did. Strong reactors also reached for fewer tactics, a sign of lower effort. The authors borrow the airplane rule for their advice: settle your own feelings first, then turn to the other person's. The finding matters for support work, care roles, and close bonds alike.
pmc-13583067:
Donna Ruth, Margaret Hammersla, and Andrea Tanner report a 2026 quality project from a rural elementary school in Montana. Children with anxiety often show up at the school health office with aches that have no clear cause. The school nurse began watching for pupils who came in three or more times in six weeks with such complaints. Those pupils were then offered a standard anxiety check, filled in by both the child and a parent.

Of 430 pupils, eight met the visit rule, six finished the check, and five screened positive for anxiety. Each of those five got a short talk with the nurse and a referral for counseling. The authors present the plan as a workable way for school nurses to spot anxiety early where mental health care is scarce.
pmc-13591167:
Sara Penrod, Zoe Samson, and Stephanie C Chan describe, in 2026, how 68 adults with disorders of consciousness fared in acute care after severe brain injury. Such patients range from coma to near wakefulness, and most prior work looks at later rehab stages. At a major trauma hospital the team tracked awareness with a standard recovery scale. They also tracked breathing, throat tube care, and swallowing.

On arrival most patients were in unresponsive wakefulness, yet by discharge none stayed in coma and many had emerged. Most patients with breathing tubes tried speaking valves, and over two thirds had the tube removed. Penrod and the team argue that structured checks and rehab should start in the first days, not weeks later.
pmc-13592667:
Serena Kao and three colleagues gather what remote care did for women's mental health during and after the pandemic. Phone and video therapy spread fast, yet results for women stayed scattered across small studies. Their review searched five databases through March 2026 and kept 57 studies with 13,457 women in 24 countries. Trials were pooled for depression, anxiety, and stress outcomes, while other designs fed summaries of acceptability and satisfaction.

Remote care beat waiting lists and usual care on all three outcomes. Depression improved most, with a moderate effect, anxiety close behind, and stress gains modest. Results swung widely between settings, so certainty stayed moderate. Benefits held in women only samples. Kao and the team call telehealth a scalable route to care while demanding stronger trials.
pmc-13598567:
Maitikuerban and colleagues build and validate a questionnaire that measures how people with chronic disease look for health information, a habit that shapes daily self care. Existing tools cover only active searching, missing the passive ways information reaches patients through feeds and pushes. Their 2026 study, published in Chinese, grounds the design in Wilson's model of information behavior. Items are drafted from literature and team debate, refined through expert consultation, and fielded with 368 patients across six Zhejiang cities.

The instrument holds thirty items in four dimensions: information needs, channels used, searching and obtaining, and judging what was found. Reliability ran high, and experts backed nearly every item. Factor analysis pulled out three shared factors covering three quarters of the variation, and a confirmatory model fit well. Nurses and doctors, the authors argue, now have a sound tool for spotting where a patient's information habits need coaching.
pmc-13602467:
Ting Pan and three colleagues check in 2026 whether two questionnaires measure self-directed weight stigma in women after childbirth. New mothers face intense pressure to lose pregnancy weight quickly, and turning society's weight bias inward can harm mental health. Two scales exist for this, the Weight Self-Stigma Questionnaire and the Weight Bias Internalization Scale, but neither had been validated in postpartum women. The team gave both to 476 Chinese mothers averaging about 31 years old.

Both scales proved internally consistent and tracked with body mass index, felt stigma, worse psychological outcomes, and restrained or emotional eating. Their structures differed: the self-stigma questionnaire's two-factor structure held up, while the bias scale's single-factor structure did not. The authors recommend the self-stigma questionnaire for postpartum use now. The bias scale needs revision and fresh validation before it can be trusted with new mothers.
pmc-13607567:
Rosa Gemma Viterbo and five colleagues review how the immune system may shape autism's wide variety. Autistic people differ greatly in language, attention, thinking skills, and long-term outcomes, and genetics alone does not explain the spread. Their review gathers the molecular and cellular routes by which immune disturbance and autoimmunity could modify development.

Topics range over immune activation in mothers during pregnancy, maternal antibodies reacting with the fetal brain, cytokine signaling, and brain immune cells, microglia and astrocytes. Complement-driven pruning of synapses and gut-immune-brain pathways also feature. The authors are careful: immune dysfunction looks like a modifier of autism's shape in some people, not a universal cause. Direct long-term studies tying immune profiles to thinking trajectories remain scarce, above all in adults. Joining molecular, immune, and psychological data, they argue, could define subgroups and guide biomarker work.
pmc-13614167:
Renato D. dos Santos, Guilherme Colherinhas, and Wesley B. Cardoso test in 2026 whether HIV drugs could be reused against West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne virus that can attack the brain and has no approved drug treatment. Working fully on computers, they docked ten HIV protease blockers into the virus's own protease, an enzyme it needs to copy itself, then ran motion simulations to see which drugs stayed bound.

Two drugs, indinavir and atazanavir, held on firmly, with steady contact, lasting hydrogen bonds, and favourable binding energy. Several others scored well in the still docking test yet drifted loose once the simulation moved. The lesson for drug hunting is plain: a good first fit means little until the pairing survives motion. The two winners now merit testing in real lab experiments.
pmc-13617767:
Yongbin Xu and seven colleagues describe a pectin-like polysaccharide from the pollen of Typha angustifolia, a cattail plant used in traditional medicine, and test how it steers immune cells. Plant pectins are promising immune modulators, yet their tangled makeup has hidden which parts do the work. The team mapped the molecule's size, sugar building blocks, and branching with chemical analysis and magnetic resonance methods, then exposed mouse dendritic cells to it.

The polysaccharide, about ten kilodaltons in size, mixes smooth pectin regions with richly branched side chains and rare structural motifs. It matured dendritic cells without poisoning them, raising surface activation markers and inflammatory signals while reducing their appetite for swallowing particles. Treated cells then activated antigen-specific killer T cells more strongly, boosting their growth and interferon output. Tests against clipped versions suggest the intact, complex branching underlies the activity, though molecule size may also play a part.
pmc-13618067:
Mansoore Shahabi and two colleagues build a magnetic nanocatalyst pairing nickel and copper for two jobs: converting toxic nitroaromatic compounds into useful amines, and forming carbon-nitrogen bonds in a single pot. Industrial nitro compounds pollute water and resist breakdown, while their amine products feed dyes, drugs, and polymers. The catalyst sits on silica-coated magnetite particles, so a magnet can fish it out afterward.

A battery of imaging and analysis methods confirmed the layered structure. Reactions ran in water, a green solvent, finished within about two hours, and gave high yields. The nickel-copper pairing outperformed what either metal suggests alone, a synergy the authors credit for the activity. Most importantly for practical use, the catalyst survived seven consecutive runs of nitro reduction without significant loss of activity, supporting the design as a cost-effective, environmentally friendlier route to amine chemistry.
pmc-13618267:
Nicole Lardini Freitas and eight colleagues profile spinal fluid proteins in COVID-19 patients with acute neurological problems, hunting for the biology behind them. They compared patients grouped as stubborn headache alone, encephalopathy, or inflammatory brain disease, against controls with non-inflammatory conditions. Protein patterns were read for the processes they reveal.

Altered proteins clustered around the complement system, an immune attack cascade, plus microglia and macrophage activity, inflammation, and nerve-cell housekeeping. Complement and clotting cascades were switched on, with raised levels of two complement products backing the signal. Synaptic pruning pathways appeared in the encephalopathy and inflammatory groups. The inflammatory group also showed glial activation and immune cells moving into the brain, plus more microglia-related proteins. The authors propose that complement-driven inflammation, driven by glial cells, disrupts the blood-brain barrier and produces these distinct syndromes.
pmc-13618767:
Xunzhuo Dong and seven colleagues separate the effect of soil acidity itself from everything else that changes when farmers swap some synthetic fertilizer for organic amendments. Using two complementary global field datasets, they partitioned how much soil carbon gain and yield gain trace specifically to pH moving toward neutral, rather than to the added carbon or other shifts.

Organic substitution consistently nudged pH toward neutrality in acidic, neutral, and alkaline soils alike. The pH improvement alone explained fifteen percent of carbon accrual in acidic soils, about nine percent in neutral soils, and about four percent in alkaline soils, working mainly by boosting microbial biomass. That pH-linked carbon gain underpinned yield rises of roughly five to nine percent across soil types, strongest and most durable in acidic soils and peaking regionally in Africa. The authors urge pairing organic substitution with deliberate pH management.
pmc-13618967:
Dayou Cui and five colleagues build a lightweight neural network that diagnoses bearing faults in rotating machinery under noise and changing speeds. Bearings account for roughly half of rotating machinery failures, yet harsh conditions defeat many models. Their design, MDW-Mamba, decouples noise from fault features in stages. A three-channel input, a multi-scale convolution backbone, and a dual-scale wavelet module model long-range patterns efficiently.

Across three public variable-speed datasets, the network beat current best methods and kept average accuracy above eighty-seven percent even when noise exceeded signal. It does this with about a quarter-million parameters and answers in about a millisecond. That is small and fast enough for real-time diagnosis on small edge devices mounted on the machines. The authors position it for wind turbines, aerospace propulsion, and heavy manufacturing, where catching a failing bearing early prevents downtime and loss.
pmc-13619067:
Andrew J. Webb and seven colleagues show that chewing sugary gum can amplify beetroot juice's blood-pressure benefit, in a 2026 crossover experiment. Dietary nitrate is concentrated in saliva, where tongue bacteria convert it to nitrite, the step to vessel-relaxing nitric oxide. Fourteen volunteers drank a beetroot shot on two visits, chewing either sugary acidic bubble gum or sugar-free gum, and were tracked for seven hours.

The sugary gum dropped salivary acidity, by one and a half pH units. Nitrate delivery did not change, yet salivary nitrite production jumped forty-five percent and plasma nitrite rose a quarter, showing mouth bacteria work faster in acid conditions. Blood pressure followed: systolic fell nearly three points and diastolic nearly two, both significant. The authors note the trick could potentiate other nitrate benefits, such as exercise performance. It reframes an everyday habit, gum choice, as a lever on a body pathway.
pmc-13619567:
Hannah Meinert led a large team searching for a brain wiring pattern tied to social anxiety across diagnoses. Social anxiety runs on a spectrum, from mild shyness in healthy people to a full disorder. The researchers scanned 160 participants across that spectrum and rebuilt each person's structural connectome, the map of white-matter links between brain regions.

A predictive modeling method found a network of forty-six connections whose pattern tracked how socially anxious each person was, regardless of diagnosis. Key hub regions sat in visual and parietal areas and in part of the frontal lobe. Sixty-four participants had social anxiety disorder and ninety-six did not, and the shared network still held across the groups. The authors present the result as early evidence that one brain network underlies social anxiety wherever it appears on the spectrum.
pmc-13620167:
Kyungbin Yoo and eight colleagues built a brain stimulator for mice that runs entirely on radio waves, with no battery and no wires. Tools for nudging brain circuits in freely moving animals usually need batteries or special cages wrapped in power coils. Their device pairs a flexible antenna that catches radio-frequency power from almost any angle with circuits that turn it into steady direct current for stimulation.

In mice moving freely around a normal cage, the device held its output voltage steady for most of the session, dipping only briefly when a mouse twisted sharply. Aimed at a motor area of the cortex, the stimulation reliably made mice circle, proving the current reached the brain with behavioral effect. The authors say radiative power transfer can free neurostimulation experiments from tethers and coil-lined arenas.
pmc-13620267:
Zikang Guo, Yunwen Wu, Yuhui Guo, and Shenghong Ju introduce Q-LEAP, a design system that uses quantum annealing to invent optical metamaterials, artificial structures that steer light in ways natural materials cannot. The search space is enormous, holding more design candidates than any team could test one by one. A factorization machine first learns the landscape, then quantum tunneling jumps across it to promising corners.

One optimization step finished in a few milliseconds and landed close to the theoretical best score for the target. By the team's combined measure of speed, sampling, and quality, the system beat the best conventional optimizer by a wide margin. A physics-guided machine learning partner predicted how candidate materials respond across the light spectrum, extending reliable estimates beyond the cutoff of standard calculations. The target design emits selectively in one infrared band while suppressing others, a trick useful for heat management.
pmc-13620867:
Pan Li and eleven colleagues ran a randomized trial of 5G cloud follow-up for heart failure patients living far from specialist centers. These patients carry implanted defibrillators that need regular checks and sometimes remote reprogramming. Two hundred six patients at five centers were assigned to a year of remote platform care or standard clinic visits.

The remote group got help far sooner after a clinical event, with response time cut from well over a week to a few days on median. Quality of life scores improved more in the remote group at twelve months. Unplanned visits and intervention rates matched between groups, and no complications came from the remote procedures. The platform links community hospitals to implant centers over 5G, so specialists can direct care while patients stay local. The authors call it a workable model for underserved regions.
pmc-13621467:
Adam Daly and five colleagues, writing as early-career researchers joined by an experienced public contributor, examine why involving patients and the public in research is hard at the start of a career. Done badly, involvement becomes token decoration that shuts contributors out. The authors organize the problem into three areas: teaching, practice, and data governance.

On teaching, they argue involvement belongs inside research training itself, with patients helping to teach it. On practice, thin budgets and narrow recruitment shut out diverse voices, so they push creative methods that meet people where they are. On data, junior researchers often feel lost deciding ownership and safety with contributors, so the paper proposes a framework for working those questions through together. Their shared message: the barriers are real, yet each one hides a workable opening.
pmc-13621567:
Xiaochen Ji, Zhiqiang Niu, and Yabo Wang report a suspected nerve injury following a stellate ganglion block given for stubborn insomnia. The procedure injects local anesthetic beside a neck nerve cluster to calm the autonomic nervous system, and its use has spread into sleep medicine. Their patient, a forty-nine-year-old woman, felt radiating shoulder pain the moment the block was placed.

Her right upper arm went numb on its outer side and her deltoid muscle weakened, a pattern pointing to the fifth cervical nerve root. Electrical testing of muscle and nerve supported an acute injury at that root. The authors stop short of claiming proof, since timing alone cannot establish that the needle caused the damage. They use the case to press practical cautions: watch the needle tip continuously under imaging, halt at the first radiating pain, check neurology promptly, and report uncertainty honestly when publishing complications.
pmc-13623367:
Nevin Karakus, Elif Donmezoglu Kutukcu, and Sumeyye Yildirim look for blood signals that warn of pregnancy complications, using tiny gene regulators called microRNAs that float in the mother's blood. Such markers could one day allow a simple blood test instead of waiting for symptoms. The prospective study ran at a university clinic in Tokat, Türkiye.

Thirty-nine pregnant women took part: twenty-eight healthy and eleven with complications, split between blood pressure disorders and pregnancy diabetes. Lab tests measured two candidate microRNAs in plasma. One of them, MIR375-3p, ran clearly lower in women with complications than in healthy women, while the other showed no firm difference. The authors propose the lowered marker as a possible early indicator worth pursuing. They are candid about the small group size and call for larger studies before any test could be trusted in practice.
pmc-13623467:
Reinhilde Jacobs, Rellyca Sola Gracea, and Dhanaporn Papasratorn published a 2026 commentary on the images behind artificial intelligence in dentistry. Most dental AI tools learn from scans and X-rays, and the authors ask whether those training images are good enough for the claims made. With dentists scarce worldwide, the pressure to automate is real.

The authors sort dental imaging by task. For single-tooth X-rays, taken and read in seconds, they warn that AI overlays and boxes can hide the fine detail that makes the image useful. Panoramic views, which show the whole jaw at once, present a different balance of risks and gains. Three-dimensional scans add another case. Their common thread is that image quality, fit to the task, and honest clinical testing decide whether a tool helps or distracts. At present, they say, those conditions are rarely met, so enthusiasm should wait on proof.
pmc-13623667:
Thomas Murchie, writing alone, works out a maths puzzle about effective arterial elastance, a single number summarising the load the arteries place on the heart. Older formulas split that load into a resistance part and a stiffness part joined by a fudge factor, yet published values for the factor disagree, and some studies claim stiffness barely matters.

Murchie derives a cleaner approximation from a model of the arterial tree by simplifying its exponential term. The result says the fudge factor is not fixed: it grows with the share of each heartbeat spent in diastole, the resting phase, squared and halved. He checked the formula across hundreds of combinations of resistance, stiffness, and heart rate in a virtual population numbering more than four thousand adults from a vessel model. The approximation tracked the full model exactly and beat earlier versions. The work explains why past estimates scattered.
pmc-13623767:
Chiara Paolin and colleagues study brain injury found before heart surgery in children with complex congenital heart disease at the University of Padova in Italy. Such injuries, present from fetal or newborn life, predict later development problems. The team compared children with genetic syndromes against those without, a group rarely separated in earlier work.

Fifty-four children who had brain scans before surgery between January 2020 and October 2024 were followed, with development checks up to eighteen months. Brain lesions appeared in forty-four percent overall, and rates were similar in syndromic and non-syndromic children. Stroke in an artery was the most common lesion, followed by bleeding under the skull and clots in brain veins. Syndromic children, though, had rockier newborn courses and clearly worse development, above all in movement and language. The authors conclude that the syndrome itself, not extra brain injury, drives the added risk.
pmc-13626167:
Weidong Jin and co-authors build a sensor that sniffs out pancreatic cancer from a droplet of blood fluid. Tumors shed tiny parcels called exosomes, and catching them early could save lives in a cancer usually found too late. Their probe pairs two grippers. Magnetic beads carry one antibody, and MXene sheets, a flaky conductive material, carry another. The pair grips matching parcels in a sandwich, and a terahertz metasurface reads the catch with boosted resonance.

The sensor found as few as hundreds of parcels per milliliter, beating gold particles as an amplifier. In mice it tracked early tumors and treatment response, and in sixty people it separated patients from healthy controls almost perfectly, outscoring the standard CA19-9 blood test in early-stage cases. Ten microliters and a few dollars per test make the design clinic-friendly.
pmc-13627867:
Jaqueline Hersch-González and colleagues compare three lineages of the laboratory worm Caenorhabditis elegans to learn what decades on the bench do to a model animal. Their panel joins a fresh isolate from Mexico City, the standard N2 strain kept in labs today, and an ancestral N2 line frozen since 1969. Life history, stress survival, and gene activity were measured side by side under the same conditions.

The Mexican worms lived shorter lives and bred less, yet survived a bacterial pathogen better, while the ancestral line shrugged off oxidative stress but wilted in heat. Gene profiles of the Mexican and ancestral strains resembled each other more than either resembled today's N2, and only a small core of heat shock genes answered in all three. Strain history, the authors warn, is a hidden variable in worm experiments.
pmc-13628567:
Ivan Šitum and eight colleagues pooled trial evidence on two ways of keeping day-surgery patients asleep. One way gives the drug propofol through a vein. The other uses sevoflurane gas. Their review gathered fifteen trials with 1,345 adults having outpatient surgery. The trials came out between 2014 and 2025. The team compared waking speed, sickness, and pain after surgery.

Patients on vein propofol had far less sickness and vomiting after surgery. They also reported slightly lower pain scores. Waking told a mixed story, though. One trial found faster readiness to go home. Time in the recovery unit did not differ overall. Waking times varied too much to pool. The authors advise picking the method by patient needs and local resources. Neither way wins clearly on speed.
pmc-13629567:
Zhilei Zhang and two colleagues examined 104 Chinese college students. They untangled how body size, grip strength, and bone density connect. Skeletal muscle was the suspected middleman. Students are still building peak bone mass. The team measured forearm bone density. They also measured height, weight, grip strength, and muscle mass.

All the measures moved together in a positive way. Modelling then showed that muscle carried a real share of the effect. Both body weight and grip strength acted on bone density through muscle. Sex predicted muscle mass directly. It did not predict bone density itself. Height showed no indirect route through muscle once sex was counted. The authors conclude that building and keeping muscle is a practical lever. It can mean stronger bones in young adults.
pmc-13629767:
Miao-Miao Chen and six colleagues assembled the full mitochondrial genome of Rhynocoris altaicus. This predatory assassin bug of the eastern Palearctic hunts moth and butterfly pests. The work supplies the first full genetic reference for this wide-ranging species. Its kin help control pests in farms and forests.

The circular genome runs just over sixteen thousand DNA letters. It is rich in adenine and thymine. It carries the standard thirty-seven mitochondrial genes plus a control region. Family tree analysis used thirteen protein-coding genes. It placed Rhynocoris as the closest kin of Sphedanolestes within its subfamily. That confirms earlier hints from the one published relative. The sequence sits in a public database. Workers in taxonomy, evolution, and conservation can use it.
pmc-13633467:
Anne-Marie Roque-Afonso and seven colleagues, writing for the Demosthenes research group, tracked hepatitis A severity in French hospitals from 2013 to 2024. Hepatitis A is a liver infection spread through contaminated food, water, or close contact. It usually passes mildly in children but hits adults harder. As infections fall across Europe, cases shift to older ages where danger grows. The team used the national hospital discharge database to find every admitted case.

Nearly eight thousand cases were identified, with a median age of thirty. Well over a quarter developed severe disease with organ failure, and a small share died. Older age, male sex, smoking, and existing liver problems raised the odds of severity. Death tied most strongly to heavy overall illness burden and to cirrhosis. Severe disease and death both grew more common in the most recent period. The authors suggest wider, perhaps universal, vaccination deserves consideration.
pmc-13634267:
Pavlina Lenga and six colleagues reviewed outcomes for patients with cerebral cavernous malformations at one large center. These tangles of blood vessels in the brain can bleed, yet removing them carries its own risks. Doctors lack solid rules for choosing between watching and operating. The team analyzed two hundred sixty-eight patients treated between 2014 and 2021, recording symptoms, scans, treatments, complications, and daily function scores.

Most patients arrived after a bleed, and most were managed without surgery. About a quarter of the treated group had operations, usually within seven weeks of diagnosis. Roughly a quarter of surgical patients suffered a new neurological complication afterward. Function scores in the surgical group improved by last follow-up, except that brainstem lesions left deeper disability. Bleeds during watchful waiting were rare in the recorded years. The authors say the numbers support careful, case-by-case choices rather than any single rule.
pmc-13635467:
Daiki Hatakeyama and colleagues studied how the liver expels its own injured cells. The liver keeps itself healthy both by regrowing tissue and by pushing abnormal liver cells out into the blood channels, where they die and get eaten by scavenger cells. A growth switch called YAP marks the cells chosen for expulsion. The team read the gene activity of such cells and mapped which DNA regions stood open in them.

The doomed cells switched on genes for halting division and reshaping their skeletons. They also released signals that summon and activate the scavenger macrophages. Open DNA regions clustered around binding sites for a shape-organizing protein called CTCF. Lab tests showed the YAP partnership physically associates with that protein in the nucleus. The authors describe a three-part axis that remodels DNA packaging to run the expulsion program, a fresh angle on how livers stay clean.
pmc-13637267:
Kil Yong Choi and Ho-Hyun Kim published this 2026 cohort study of air pollution and illness near industrial zones in South Korea's Gyeonggi province. Residents breathe emissions from big plants and small workshops alike. The team modeled how particles drift on local winds and linked exposure to national health records. Winds blew mostly from the west and northwest, letting coarse particles pile up near the complexes.

Peak particle levels in the worst season far exceeded the annual standard. Respiratory illness struck the exposed population clearly more often than the comparison group. One oddity ran the other way: rhinitis rates were sky high in both groups and slightly higher in the control area. The authors still read the pattern as long-term industrial exposure raising respiratory risk, with possible cancer and chronic disease links. They offer the work as baseline data for environmental health policy in industrial regions.
pmc-13638767:
Courtney E. Harris and eight colleagues wrote a 2026 field report on starting a career in transplant infectious diseases. This small specialty deals with infections in patients whose immune systems are weakened by organ transplant treatment.

Drawing on their own early years, the authors cover mentorship, training junior doctors, building skills, and choosing research projects. They also discuss time management during unpredictable clinical work, keeping up with new science, and staying visible in a transplant team. Their shared theme is that young specialists must align clinical, academic, and personal goals deliberately if they want lasting impact rather than mere survival.
pmc-13639067:
Manu Suvarna and eight colleagues describe a 2026 project that fine-tunes a large language model to write recipes for single-atom catalysts. These catalysts, with isolated metal atoms on a support, are hard to design because knowledge sits scattered across fast-growing literature.

The team trained the model on 2,964 publications and built an interface where researchers request procedures by metal, support, and target reaction. Human reviewers checked 150 generated protocols and found the steps coherent and chemically sensible, though with clear limits. The authors stress that model output must be reviewed critically and used as an assistant, not an authority.
pmc-13641967:
Maria Fernanda Silva Andrade-Bortoletto and six colleagues present a 2026 laboratory study comparing two imaging routes for finding a hidden second root canal in lower front teeth. Missing such a canal is a known cause of root canal treatment failure, and a nearby zirconia implant might distort the images.

Twenty extracted incisors, some with one canal and some with two, were set in a human jaw beside an implant. Five evaluators read angled X-ray pairs and two cone-beam scan protocols. All routes performed comparably, and the implant did not reduce accuracy. The authors say the simpler X-ray technique remains a valid choice here.
pmc-13642367:
