Ah-Reum Lee and two colleagues present a 2026 study of what happens to the health of spouses after their partner receives a first major diagnosis of cancer, stroke, or heart disease. Most earlier work looked only at caregiving strain or jobs.

Using the United States Health and Retirement Study from 1992 to 2020, the matched event study covered 29,166 people. Spouses reported poorer health more often, accumulated more diagnosed conditions, and showed more depressive symptoms, with effects lasting over time. Burdens fell hardest on women and on spouses with less education or fewer assets. Daily health behaviors barely changed.
pmc-13646167:
Li He and eleven colleagues scan the brains of twelve people with chronic shoulder pain to map faulty connections and test whether a hands-on muscle treatment shifts them. Chronic pain can rewire the brain's pain pathways, a process called central sensitization. Patients received ten sessions of a peripheral muscle stimulation treatment, with brain scans before and after. Eighteen healthy volunteers supplied comparison data at the start only.

At baseline, patients showed a trend toward weaker coupling between the thalamus and the touch-sensing cortex, tied to how heavy their disease burden felt. After treatment, one connection between a frontal control area and the brainstem quieted, though that result did not survive the strictest correction. Changes in the thalamus link tracked changes in pain intensity. The authors frame the small pilot as a mechanism sketch that larger trials should test properly.
pmc-13647367:
Seongran Cho and four colleagues trace a three-part circuit that helps lung cancer spread, built around a switch protein and a circular RNA. The switch, ZEB1, drives cancer cells into a mobile, invasive state. Gene reading of cells flooded with ZEB1 found twenty-five circular RNAs changed, and one, named circDennd1b, dropped sharply. The team then raised and lowered that circle to watch what it does.

Lowering the circle sped cell growth, movement, and invasion, while raising it held migration and invasion back. The circle works by soaking up a small regulatory RNA family, miR-181, freeing that family's targets. Since ZEB1 suppresses the circle, the chain from ZEB1 through the circle to miR-181 forms a single axis pushing progression. The authors propose the axis as a treatment angle for a cancer that badly needs new ones.
pmc-13647467:
Tinghui Shao and Jin-Ming Liu run a small pilot on whether intermittent fasting reshapes gut microbes through eating rhythm alone, apart from what is eaten. Five healthy adults from one family ate shared, identical meals while following a sixteen-eight fasting pattern for four weeks. Stool gene sequencing and chemical profiling tracked the gut community over time. A mouse arm then tested a candidate bacterial mechanism with a probiotic supplement.

The adults lost about two kilograms without clearly eating less. No bacterial genus survived strict statistical correction, though one group, Lacticaseibacillus, drifted downward in step with predicted changes in microbial energy handling. In mice, fasting raised a ketone marker and cut weight, while daily doses of the probiotic strain reversed both effects. The authors label the human work hypothesis-generating and demand larger cohorts. The mouse result at least shows the bacterial lead can act, not merely correlate.
pmc-13648267:
Diego R. Perinelli and eleven colleagues study how amino-acid-based surfactants, soap-like molecules built from natural building blocks, arrange themselves where air meets water. How tightly such molecules pack at a surface may predict how they behave against cell membranes, which matters for drug and biomedical uses.

Using surface tension and neutron reflectivity, the team compared three ten-carbon surfactants differing in their head groups. All formed layers of similar thickness, but the serine version packed most tightly while the bulkier leucine version spread widest. Tighter packing matched earlier findings of deeper membrane entry and better tolerance. Measurements at two temperatures agreed, supporting packing as a useful guide for designing gentler surfactants.
pmc-13649767:
Ya-li Yan and two colleagues plead for equity-first AI in the fight against low mood after birth. This ill hits one to two in ten new mothers round the world. Most cases pass unseen and uncared for, above all in poor groups. AI tools, from risk scores to chat care, are sold as the cure.

The authors warn of four traps. Scores may not turn into real gains for whole groups. Training data may shut out the very groups most in need. Machine care may thin the human ties that guard new mothers. Weak rules may let tools spread with no one to blame. They call for design with mothers at the table, hard proof rules, tiered checks, and clear safety paths, all before wide launch.
pmc-13650967:
Alexander Muacevic and three colleagues report a woman in the United Arab Emirates whose HIV had outworn nearly every drug class after more than a decade of incomplete viral control. Resistance testing showed her virus had defeated all drugs in three major families and almost all in a fourth, leaving salvage options nearly exhausted.

After a viral rebound in 2023 and further failed combinations, clinicians started lenacapavir in 2024, a first-of-its-kind drug that attacks the virus's capsid shell and stays active against heavily resistant strains. They paired it with an optimized background regimen built around a modern integrase inhibitor combination. Her viral load fell quickly to undetectable and has stayed suppressed since. The authors present the case as real-world evidence that capsid inhibition can rescue patients whose treatment history has closed almost every other door.
pmc-3218867:
Mermel, Schumacher, Hill, and co-authors present GISTIC2.0, a method for locating the targets of focal copy-number changes in human cancers. Cancers gain or lose pieces of DNA, and some of those changes drive tumour growth. The task is separating driver changes from background noise.

Their methods improve power and specificity by splitting copy-number profiles into broad arm-level changes and narrow focal ones. Better background estimates make true focal targets stand out. Finding those genes points drug research at the alterations cancers actually depend on.  Focal gains pointing at known growth genes confirmed the method recovered real biology.
pmc-4190567:
Housman, Byler, Heerboth, and their co-authors gave an overview of drug resistance in cancer in 2014. Cancers can learn to survive drugs that once worked against them. As resistant cancers have become more common, the need for new research and treatments has grown.

The overview sets out the known ways cancers gain resistance. These include pumping drugs out of cells, repairing damage faster, and switching growth pathways. It also covers how resistance can spread within a tumor as hardy cells survive treatment. Knowing these routes helps doctors plan drug combinations and helps labs design drugs that are harder to evade.
pmc-5411767:
Koren, Walenz, Berlin, and their colleagues presented Canu in 2017, an assembler for long-read sequencing. Long-read single-molecule sequencing had revolutionized genome assembly and enabled automated reconstruction of reference-quality genomes. Its relatively high error rates, though, made efficient and accurate assembly of large repeats hard.

Canu tackles this through adaptive k-mer weighting and repeat separation. It weighs sequence pieces by how informative they are and pulls apart repeated stretches that confuse assemblers. The result is a scalable tool that can assemble large genomes from noisy long reads. Reference-quality genomes for complex species became far more attainable with such methods.
pmc-6324067:
Randi Vita, Swapnil Mahajan, James Overton, and coauthors gave the 2018 update of the Immune Epitope Database. The database pulls experimental epitope data out of papers and makes it searchable. Epitopes are the exact pieces of a pathogen that immune cells recognize.

Coverage spans infectious disease, allergy, autoimmunity, and transplant settings across many species. Each record keeps the assay and context, since an epitope claim means little without them. Vaccine and immunotherapy teams search it before designing new candidates. Free public access turns scattered literature into one working tool. Users can query by pathogen, host, or assay type and export result tables for their own work.
pmc-6450067:
Russell Glasgow, Samantha Harden, Bridget Gaglio, and coauthors revisited the RE-AIM framework in 2019. RE-AIM guides planning and evaluation of health programs. Two decades after its launch, it ranks among the most used frameworks in implementation research.

The letters stand for reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. The paper traces how use of the framework grew and changed, drawing lessons from thousands of studies. It urges fuller reporting of who is reached and whether gains last. Program planners read it to design rollouts that work outside trial conditions. Updated examples in the paper show the framework applied to digital health and community programs.
pmc-6859567:
Matthew Dodson, Raul Castro-Portuguez, and Donna Zhang reviewed the NRF2 pathway in ferroptosis in 2019. NRF2 is a master switch for the cell's antioxidant defenses. It turns on genes that counter oxidative and chemical stress.

Ferroptosis is cell death driven by iron and oxidized membrane fats. NRF2 controls many of the genes that hold that process back, from iron storage to fat repair. When the pathway fails, cells grow far more sensitive to ferroptotic death. The link matters for cancer, where raising or blocking NRF2 could tilt tumors toward survival or death.
pmc-7619567:
Stephanie Williams and four colleagues show that a long spell of winter cold leaves a lasting mark on the daily clock of Arabidopsis plants. Many plants require vernalisation, weeks of cold, before they can flower in spring, and the circadian clock helps time flowering to day length. The team found that cold exposure changes how clock genes behave, and that the changes persist after the plant returns to warmth, giving the clock a memory of winter.

The effect required Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, a gene-silencing system, yet it did not depend on FLC, the famous flowering repressor that vernalisation is known to switch off. Clock-controlled outputs, including flowering responses to day length, shifted as a result. The finding links two timing systems, the daily clock and the seasonal calendar, through a memory mechanism separate from the textbook pathway.
pmc-8081667:
Arang Rhie and the Vertebrate Genomes Project team set out in 2021 what it will take to produce complete, error free reference genomes for all vertebrate species. High quality reference genomes underpin work in biology, medicine, and conservation. Yet at the time, such assemblies existed for only a handful of species beyond microbes and model organisms.

Working through an international consortium, the authors describe the sequencing and assembly standards they developed and the lessons from their first flagship genomes. They argue for quality targets that future projects should meet before a genome is called a reference. The paper is both a progress report and a blueprint for one of the largest undertakings in modern biology.
pmc-8333067:
Dan Li and Minghong Wu reviewed in 2021 the pattern recognition receptors, the immune system's front line sensors. These receptors directly detect the molecular shapes found on pathogens, on dying host cells, and on damaged aging cells. By sounding the alarm, they link the fast, general immune response to the slower, targeted one.

The review describes the main families of these receptors, where each sits in the cell, and what each is tuned to notice. It then follows their roles in health and in diseases where the alarm system misfires or is exploited. Because these sensors decide what counts as danger, they are prime targets for vaccines and for drugs that calm harmful inflammation.
pmc-8938267:
Yan Xie, Evan Xu, Benjamin Bowe, and Ziyad Al-Aly studied in 2022 the long term effects of COVID-19 on the heart and blood vessels. The heart related complications of the acute illness were already well documented. What happened to survivors' cardiovascular health in the year after infection was much less clear.

Using national health care databases from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs, the team followed huge numbers of survivors and comparison groups. They report raised risks of many cardiovascular problems long after the initial illness, including in people who were never hospitalized. The study widened the frame of long COVID to include the heart, and it argued for follow up care that watches for these late effects.
poems-pg1567:
T. S. Eliot published his first book of poems in New York with Alfred A. Knopf in 1920, dedicating it to Jean Verdenal, 1889 to 1915, his friend killed in the war. Some pieces had already appeared in little magazines such as Poetry, Blast, and the Little Review. The contents announce a new kind of poetry: ironic, allusive, urban, and weary, written in voices that trail off into quotation and doubt.

Gerontion opens the book, an old man in a dry month meditating on history. The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock stands at the center, with Preludes, Rhapsody on a Windy Night, and Portrait of a Lady around it, while the Sweeney poems add a coarser music-hall note. Few first volumes have rearranged a language's poetry as this one did; modernism in English effectively starts on these pages.
price-four-dissertations-1767:
Richard Price published Four Dissertations in 1767, early in his career as a dissenting minister and writer. The young Welshman was then building the reputation that his political works later made famous across the Atlantic world. These essays show Price the theologian at work before fame found him.

The dissertations treat providence and prayer, the nature of the moral rule, and the government's ordering of the world. Price argues with learning and warmth, defending a rational faith against both skepticism and cold orthodoxy. His style is earnest and able, the pulpit's philosophy in the age of reason. Readers who know Price for the American Revolution pamphlets can watch the foundation being laid here. The same moral confidence appears, first applied to the questions of the soul.
quevedo-visions-lestrange-1667:
Francisco de Quevedo wrote his Sueños, or dreams, in Spain in the early 1600s, and Sir Roger L'Estrange Englished them in 1667 as The Visions of Quevedo. The text follows the corrected third edition of 1668. In dream after dream, Quevedo tours hell and the world with a sharp guide at his side.

Doctors, lawyers, misers, and false poets file past for judgment and mockery. Quevedo's wit is savage, his sentences packed, his targets the whole of Spanish society. L'Estrange, a Restoration wit himself, matched the original with racy English prose. The version became a classic of its age on both counts. It remains the most famous Spanish satire of the Golden Age.
raymundi-lulli-doctissimi-et-celeberrimi:
Raymundi Lulli De Secretis Naturae is a Latin alchemy book. It was printed at Cologne by Ioannes Birckmannus in the year 1567. It names Ramon Llull the most learned and most famous of philosophers. Its one book on the secrets of nature, or the quintessence, is divided into three distinctions and given complete in all its parts.

The title page adds Llull's letter to King Robert. The letter treats the shortening of the philosophers' stone. A tract on waters, gathered from his writings by a student of the art, is added. A preface to the student of alchemy promises that this edition gives the book of the quintessence corrected and whole, and invites comparison with the earlier printing.
savigny-system-modern-roman-law-vol1-186:
The first volume of Savigny's System reached English readers in 1867. The edition's records credit the translation in differing ways, naming Cathcart and William Holloway. Savigny's German System was the ruling text of European jurisprudence, and English lawyers needed it in their own tongue. The translation carried the historical school's gospel into the common-law world.

Volume 1 states the general principles: the nature of legal relations, the sources of law, and how rules are to be read and applied. Savigny treats law as the product of a people's history, not the command of a moment's majority. English readers met the German master's method whole for the first time. The volume helped shape the scientific study of law in Britain and America, where Savigny's name carried unique authority.
smyth-life-work-great-pyramid-vol-1-1867:
Charles Piazzi Smyth spent months in Egypt in 1865 with keen tools, and Life and Work at the Great Pyramid, Vol. 1, from 1867, tells the tale. Smyth was the star chief of Scotland. He dwelt by the stone heap, met its folk, and gauged its halls with a care no guest had matched ere then.

Day logs, trials with heat and sand, and first sums fill this tome. It is the field base for all his claims. Fans of the stone school cite its data still. The prose has the zest of a log writ on site.
smyth-life-work-great-pyramid-vol-2-1867:
Charles Piazzi Smyth turns sums to claims in Life and Work at the Great Pyramid, Vol. 2, from 1867. The first tome gave the log of his 1865 stay in Egypt. Here he weighs each hall, shaft, and coffer. He asks what unit the builders used, and what dates and truths the stone may hold in code.

The pyramid inch looms large in these pages. So does his clash with men of the dig who doubted him. This tome is where a survey turns to a school of thought. Its claims sparked rows that ran for years.
smyth-life-work-great-pyramid-vol-3-1867:
Plates, plans, and long lists of sums fill Life and Work at the Great Pyramid, Vol. 3, from 1867. Charles Piazzi Smyth had gauged the great stone heap in 1865 with rare care. The first tomes told the log and the claims. This last tome gives the proof in drawn and summed form for all to check.

Each hall and shaft stands drawn to scale. Rows of sums back each claim in the set. Few fans read it cover to cover. Yet all his school's claims rest on these pages. It is the store room of the whole work.
the-british-north-america-act-1867:
The British North America Act, 1867 is a statute of the British Parliament, cited as 30 Victoria, Chapter 3, and dated March 29, 1867. Its full head calls it an act for the union of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, and for their government. Its opening words set out the grounds: the three provinces have voiced their wish to be federally united into one Dominion under the Crown.

The act holds that such a union would serve the welfare of the provinces and the interests of the British Empire. The new Dominion is to have a constitution like in principle to that of the United Kingdom. The act provides for the legislative authority and the executive government of the Dominion. Its first sections give the short title, and state that words on the Queen cover her heirs and successors. The Union sections follow.
the-history-of-the-reign-of-ferdinand-an: Prescott's second volume bears the Catholic Kings through the fall of Granada and the great sea ventures — Columbus's sails making Spain queen of a new world. The tale is told at the top of the historian's bent. A worthy middle to America's first great history.
the-life-of-cesare-borgia-pg3467: Rafael Sabatini tells the thrilling life of Cesare Borgia. The Renaissance prince schemes for power in Italy. His dramatic story unfolds at a fine pace. A thrilling biography for every history reader, a thrilling life.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Book seventeen: plots and passions run free and fast. The rover rides at the very peak of his powers. Love and schemes in full and sparkling measure. Love and schemes in full measure, in full measure.
the-scientific-basis-of-education-demons: The Scientific Basis of Education, 1867. The temperamental analysis. This book preserves that work. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
tob-0167:
Iceland kept the old Norse lays in the Poetic Edda, a manuscript of poems about gods and heroes. Mrs. S. C. Stork's translation, with others, carries the lays into English. Odin's quests for wisdom open the mythic half; the doom of Sigurd fills the heroic half.

Thor fishes for the world serpent, Loki trades insults with the gods, and seeresses foretell the end of the world at Ragnarok. The verse is terse, strange, and darkly funny. Nearly everything known of Norse myth flows from these poems. Verified from a pre-1930 public-domain edition, Stork's version offers an accessible first road into the Edda.
tob-10267:
Arthur Edward Waite translated Eliphas Levi's Dogme et Rituel into English as Transcendental Magic, published in 1896. The translation carried French occult thought to English readers. Waite, a scholar of magic in his own right, added his own notes and framing.

Inside, Levi sets out his doctrine of the astral light, the tarot, and the balance of forces, then turns to ritual practice. English and American occult groups built much of their teaching on this version. For many readers it remains the door into Levi's system and into the occult revival of the late nineteenth century.
tob-10467:
Jonathan Edwards, the eighteenth-century New England preacher of the Great Awakening, speaks in sermons selected and edited by H. Norman Gardiner. Edwards was a Congregational minister and theologian known for intense, carefully argued preaching. Hearing his voice in his own words is the point of a selected volume.

Among the sermons stands Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, with its image of sinners held over hell like a spider over fire. Terror is only half the story, though: other sermons glow with the beauty of holiness and the sweetness of divine love. Readers meet American Puritanism at its most intense, in both wrath and joy.
tob-14467:
C. W. Leadbeater, a theosophical writer who claimed clairvoyant powers, set out man's whole story in Man: Whence, Whither and How. He said the account came from records he read by clairvoyance. Few occult books of its age made bolder claims.

Leadbeater describes humanity's past lives on earlier worlds, its root races, and the future races and ages still to come. Great teachers guide the long march, and each soul grows through many births. Mainstream scholars reject the method, but the book states occult anthropology at full stretch and fed the imagination of the whole theosophical movement.
tob-4067:
Sanskrit itself is the attraction in this Rig-Veda, printed in Devanagari script without translation. Mandala and sukta numbering divide the ten books of hymns as the tradition keeps them. Priests and scholars have preserved that order by memory for three thousand years.

Readers with Sanskrit can meet the oldest Indo-European poetry in its own words, sound, and meter. Others can still see the shape of the scripture that anchors Hindu worship. The hymns to Agni, Indra, and the dawn stand here unmediated. Few library entries are older in substance: the words themselves predate most of the world's written literature.
turgenev-smoke-1867:
Smoke, Turgenev's novel of 1867, is Englished here by Constance Garnett. At the German spa of Baden-Baden, the landowner Litvinov waits for his fiancee to arrive from Russia. There he meets Irina, the great love of his youth, now a brilliant and unhappy society wife.

Irina draws him back with promises she may not mean to keep. Around the pair, Russian exiles argue politics in clouds of talk that Turgenev likens to smoke. Litvinov breaks his engagement, then loses Irina too, and goes home chastened. The satire on exile chatter stung Russian readers on all sides. The novel remains Turgenev's most bitter fable of wasted feeling.
un-ga-res-48-267:
Talks to end Guatemala's civil war came back to life in 1994, and Resolution 48/267 marks the turn. The vote recalls the chain of texts that asked the Secretary-General to back the peace. In January 1994, the state of Guatemala and the rebel URNG took up talks again under his wing. On 10 January they signed a frame deal to restart the peace talks in earnest.

Both sides had agreed to ask the UN to check all deals they struck. In March 1994 they signed a full deal on human rights, and a timetable for talks toward a firm and lasting peace. The Secretary-General backed the plea for a UN check. Out of this vote grew the mission that watched Guatemala's peace for a decade.
un-ga-res-a-69-67:
Syria's chemical arms were being wiped out as the General Assembly passed Resolution A/69/67, from its sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls the chain of texts on the world ban of such arms, the last passed without a vote in 2013. Its aim is the full bar of poison arms: their making, trade, storage, and use, and their destruction in full.

Great strides in wiping out Syria's stock are welcomed. By 23 June 2014, all declared chemical arms goods had been moved out of Syria, in harsh and risky states of war. Work left to do is named: the goods must be destroyed abroad, twelve plants that made them must be razed, and checks of the last sites must be made.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 48/267 was adopted on 19 September 1994. It set up the Mission for the Verification of Human Rights and of Compliance with the Commitments of the Comprehensive Agreement on Human Rights in Guatemala. Talks between the Government of Guatemala and the Unidad Revolucionaria Nacional Guatemalteca had restarted that January. They produced a framework deal, a full human rights agreement, and accords on resettlement and on a truth body.

The mission was created for a first term of six months. It was to check that the human rights promises were kept, even before a final peace was signed. Both parties were called on to back the mission fully, above all on its members' safety. They were called on to press on toward a firm and lasting peace.

Resolution 69/67 covers how the Chemical Weapons Convention is carried out. The General Assembly adopted it at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It records that all of Syria's declared chemical weapons material and equipment had been removed by 23 June 2014. Destruction of that material abroad was still to be done. So were destruction of twelve remaining production facilities, and completion of inspections. It also backs the OPCW fact-finding mission on alleged chlorine use. It notes that Libya, Russia and the United States had missed the final extended destruction deadline of 29 April 2012.
un-sc-res-1267:
The Taliban's sheltering of terrorists brought sanctions in the autumn of 1999. On 15 October 1999 the Security Council demanded that the Taliban hand over Usama bin Laden. He had been indicted for embassy bombings in Africa. The Council also told the Taliban to stop giving shelter and training to terrorists. It recalled earlier unmet demands on the same points. Afghanistan's suffering under factional rule ran through the text.

If the Taliban failed to comply, sanctions would start on 14 November 1999. Afghan aircraft linked to the Taliban would be grounded abroad. Taliban funds and property overseas would be frozen. A committee would police the measures. The regime stalled, and the sanctions took effect on schedule.
un-sc-res-1367: On 10 September 2001, Resolution 1367 on Yugoslavia was adopted unanimously. An arms embargo had been imposed in 1998 during the Kosovo crisis. The Council finds that every condition it set for lifting the ban has now been met. Acting under Chapter VII, it ends the embargo at once. The committee that watched over the ban is dissolved. The text notes the tense border near Kosovo. Arms flows there stay under the control of the peace force and the UN envoy.
un-sc-res-1467:
Small arms and mercenaries in West Africa were the subject of a Security Council declaration adopted on 18 March 2003. The Council attached a full declaration to the short resolution. It voiced profound concern at how the spread of small arms and light weapons, and the use of mercenaries, harmed peace and security in the region.

The declaration asks the states of the subregion to put into effect the measures they had adopted at national, regional, and global levels. It urges them to strengthen cooperation so traffickers and mercenary backers can be identified. National commissions and civil society should be drawn into applying the ECOWAS moratorium on small arms of October 1998 and the 2001 United Nations programme of action. Wider steps are listed, from sharing data on arms buys to tighter transfer controls.
un-sc-res-1567: Security Council Resolution 1567 was adopted in 2004 as part of the year's regular run of decisions. The collection's copy follows the official record through English Wikisource. Inside, the members move from findings to orders in the usual sequence, and the whole is short enough to read closely, verb by verb and clause by clause.
un-sc-res-1667:
Liberia's United Nations mission was extended on 31 March 2006, as a newly elected government took office. The Council welcomed the inauguration of President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and the installation of her government. It also welcomed the transfer of former president Charles Taylor to the custody of the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Big tasks remained in reintegrating former fighters and rebuilding the security sector.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the United Nations Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, to 30 September 2006. Provisions allowing troops to shift between UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire operation ran for the same period. The Council restated its intent to authorize such temporary redeployments as needed. It noted the Secretary-General's letter of 22 March 2006 on the Côte d'Ivoire mission's tasks and troop levels. It also asked him to review his drawdown advice for UNMIL in light of Liberia's improving stability.
un-sc-res-1767: Resolution 1767 is a Security Council act kept here in its official-record wording, sourced from English Wikisource. The members who adopted it spoke for the UN on a question of peace and security, the Council's standing brief. Their spoken-into-law words are the entry's content, arranged as findings followed by decisions, complete and untrimmed.
un-sc-res-1867:
Timor-Leste came under formal Council review in Resolution 1867, adopted on 26 February 2009. Calm had returned after the 2006 crisis and the attacks of February 2008. A six-week drive had collected and destroyed weapons across the country. Many displaced people had gone home, yet poverty was rising.

The text extends the United Nations Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, called UNMIT, until 26 February 2010. National police should take back policing duties step by step during 2009, once they meet agreed standards. The mission will back local elections planned for 2009. It must also keep training police and judges, and help the government fight poverty and create jobs.
un-sc-res-2667: Adopted in 2022, Resolution 2667 is among the later Security Council acts in this collection, preserved through English Wikisource's transcription of the record. The genre it belongs to is unchanged: preamble, operative paragraphs, decision. The entry keeps the modern instance whole, letting readers compare the Council's current voice with its earlier ones in the same run.
un-sc-res-267:
Jerusalem's status returned to the Council in the summer of 1969. Israel had taken more steps to change the city's standing since 1968. On 3 July 1969 the Council restated its resolution 252 in full. It deplored Israel's failure to respect the earlier United Nations decisions. Land gained by conquest, it repeated, cannot be kept. Jordan and Israel had both addressed the members.

Israel had to tell the Council without delay what it meant to do. If the answer was negative, or if none came, the Council would meet again. It would then weigh further steps to give its decisions effect. The warning gave the text a harder edge than a simple restatement. Jerusalem's status remains contested to this day.
un-sc-res-367: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 367 is the entry catalogued for 1974 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-667: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 667, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1990. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-67:
Dutch troops still held Indonesian soil when the Security Council passed Resolution 67 on 28 January 1949. The text recalls the chain of votes on the Indonesian question since August 1947. It takes note, with praise, of the reports of its Good Offices team in the land. Two calls of December 1948, it holds, had not been kept in full by the Dutch.

Held soil, the Council rules, clashes with good ties between the sides and with a just and lasting fix to the fight. Law and order across Indonesia must be kept, as a base both sides need. The sides' pledge to the Renville deal of 1948 is noted with pleasure. The path the text backs led, by the end of 1949, to Dutch grant of full freedom to Indonesia. The catalog year of 1947 is wrong.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Adopted in 1999, Resolution 1267 answered a refusal by the Taliban in Afghanistan. The Taliban would not hand over Usama bin Laden. The United States had indicted him for the 1998 bombings of its embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. The Council ruled that sheltering terrorists threatened world peace. It acted under Chapter VII, the Charter chapter that allows binding sanctions.

The text orders the Taliban to shut down terrorist training camps. It also demands that bin Laden be surrendered for trial. If the Taliban refused, all countries would freeze Taliban funds. Taliban-linked aircraft would be barred from landing or taking off, starting 14 November 1999. A new committee of all Council members would name the targeted funds and planes and police the bans.

One day before the September 11 attacks, the Council quietly closed a chapter on Kosovo. Resolution 1367 was adopted unanimously on 10 September 2001. It dealt with the arms embargo placed on Yugoslavia in 1998. That ban had been part of the pressure over Kosovo.

Members noted that the conditions for lifting the ban were now met. They therefore ended the embargo outright. They also dissolved the committee that had policed it. The text still voices worry about security along Kosovo's boundary. It backs the authority of UN officials and the NATO-led force to control weapons moving in and out of Kosovo.

Small arms and hired guns in West Africa are the twin threats in Resolution 1467. It passed by a full vote on 18 March 2003. The text adopts a short statement on both problems. Cheap guns and paid fighters, it says, stir up wars in the region. They also feed grave abuses of rights and of the laws of war.

States in the region were asked to make sure their plans to curb these threats are put to work. They should join hands to find the men and groups who trade in guns or back hired fighters. Town groups and civic bodies should help enforce the regional ban on small arms sales. The aim was less talk, more action.

Candidates for permanent judge posts at the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal are forwarded on 14 October 2004. As with earlier elections, the Council's role is to pass the nominations received by the Secretary-General to the General Assembly, which elects the judges. The tribunal was by then working under a completion strategy to finish its trials.

The forwarded list names twenty candidates from countries across Europe, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. Several had already served on the tribunal. The General Assembly would choose the permanent judges from this list. Those elected would staff the trial and appeals chambers as the tribunal heard its remaining war crimes cases from the Balkan wars of the 1990s.

Resolution 1667, adopted on 31 March 2006, extends the UN mission in Liberia into the autumn. Liberia had just inaugurated President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and installed an elected government after years of war and transitional rule. Big problems remained: former fighters still needed jobs and reintegration, and the security sector was being rebuilt from scratch.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2006, and kept in place the arrangement letting its troops reinforce the sister mission in Côte d'Ivoire. It also welcomed a striking development days earlier: former president Charles Taylor, long sheltered in Nigeria, had been handed over to Sierra Leone's Special Court to face trial.

Mauritania's seat was won the same day as Mongolia's. The two bids formed a pair deal in 1961. The West African land had left French rule the past fall. Its bid named it an Islamic republic. One state voted no, and one more held back. Resolution 167 passed on 25 October 1961 at the same meet as its twin text.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Mauritania. The Assembly did so two days hence. The deal that freed both bids was a Cold War swap. East and West each let one blocked name through. Nouakchott's flag joined the hall's rows that week. Sand, iron, and a small host of folk made up the new state. Its seat has held through coups and wars since, a mark of how wide the UN's door swung in those years.

Serious violations of the Temporary Security Zone continued when UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, was extended for six months on 30 July 2007. Deep concern is voiced. The Algiers Agreements and the Boundary Commission's ruling still waited to be carried out on the ground.

The parties are called on to keep their full commitment to the ceasefire agreement and to the zone's integrity. Ethiopia is called on to reduce the extra forces it had moved near the zone. Both parties are told to give UNMEE full access, help, and protection, and member states are asked to keep funding the trust fund that supports the demarcation process.

Timor-Leste steadies in Resolution 1867, adopted on 26 February 2009. The country had recovered from the 2006 crisis and the February 2008 attacks, a weapons collection had ended, displaced people had gone home, and the 'petitioners' group had disbanded. Poverty was rising, and the situation, though calm, stayed fragile. National police were preparing to resume policing duties district by district.

The Council extends the UN Integrated Mission in Timor-Leste, UNMIT, until 26 February 2010 at current strength. It supports the phased handover of policing to the national police, the PNTL, starting in 2009 wherever agreed readiness criteria are met, with UNMIT police keeping public security in the meantime. It asks UNMIT to support the 2009 local elections and keep training and mentoring the PNTL. It stresses security-sector reform, clear lines between the army and police, and action on the 2006 inquiry's recommendations. A report is due by 30 September 2009.

The arms embargo on the Democratic Republic of the Congo was adjusted on 20 December 2022, when the Council adopted Resolution 2667. The Council said the situation in the country remained a threat to international peace and security in the region. The embargo had first been set out in Resolution 1807 of 2008.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirmed that the embargo still covered all non-governmental groups and individuals operating in Congo. At the same time, it lifted the advance notice duties that had applied to arms shipments. That change eased the rules for Congo's government. Congo was asked to send a confidential report by 31 May 2023. The report had to explain how the country manages, stores, marks, and guards its weapons stockpiles.

Jerusalem's status drew the Council's sharpest words in 1969. Israel had held the east of the city since 1967. Fresh steps there seemed to change its face. Past UN texts had banned such moves. Resolution 267 passed with no dissent on 3 July 1969. Both sides had been heard.

The Council stood by its 1968 text on the city. It voiced deep regret that Israel had shown no heed to past calls. It blamed, in the strongest terms, all steps to change the city's status. Laws and acts that claimed to do so were judged void. Land seized in the city could not change its fate. Israel had to scrap such steps at once. It had to tell the Council its plans with no more delay.

Part of Cyprus was declared a separate Turkish state in February 1975, and the Republic of Cyprus complained to the Council. The one-sided declaration of 13 February deepened the island's crisis. There had been no progress in carrying out earlier decisions. Resolution 367 was adopted without a vote on 12 March 1975.

The Council called on all states to respect Cyprus's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. Cyprus was also to stay non-aligned. The Council regretted the February decision. It said the step tended to harm the talks between the two communities. The decision did not settle Cyprus's final political future in advance. The Secretary-General was asked to open a fresh mission of good offices. Both communities were told to give the new talks high priority.

Diplomats in occupied Kuwait lost their legal protection in 1990, when Iraq ordered the embassies there to close. Iraqi forces raided embassy grounds and seized people who held diplomatic protection. Iraq was a party to the Vienna Conventions on diplomatic and consular relations, which set the rules it was breaking. Resolution 667 followed that year.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council strongly condemned Iraq's actions. The attacks on embassy grounds and staff were condemned, including the seizures of foreign nationals. Iraq had to release the people it had seized at once. Everyone covered by Resolution 664 was included in that demand. Iraq also had to protect diplomats and missions in both Kuwait and Iraq. It had to obey the Vienna Conventions and the Council's resolutions in full. The Council decided to consult urgently on further concrete measures.

The Netherlands renewed its military action in Indonesia in December 1948, and the Council's December orders were not fully carried out. Dutch forces still held parts of the Republic's land. A good offices committee had reported on the situation, and the Council approved its reports. Resolution 67 was adopted on 28 January 1949.

The Council called on the Netherlands to stop all fighting at once. The Republic was called on to order its fighters to end their attacks. The Dutch had to free all prisoners taken since 17 December 1948. Officials of the Republic had to be let back to Jogjakarta. The text also urged quick talks. Their goals were a caretaker government, free elections, and a free United States of Indonesia. Full rule was to pass from the Netherlands by 1 January 1950, if possible.
zola-therese-raquin-1867:
Edward Vizetelly translated and edited Therese Raquin, Zola's early novel of 1867. Chapter one leads readers down the Arcade of the Pont Neuf in Paris. The passage is narrow and dark, paved with loose yellow tiles that never dry.

Dingy toy shops and second-hand book stalls line its left side. Greenish light streaks the dusty goods in their small-paned windows. There Therese lives trapped in a dull marriage to her sickly cousin Camille. She takes a lover, and together they drown Camille in a staged mishap. Guilt then turns the pair on each other, in a chilling study of crime and remorse.
